title: Common Skin Diseases in Primary Care

topics.SYS: Skin in diabetes, diabetic foot & thyroid

cards.q: Macule vs patch: how are they defined and what are classic examples?
cards.a:
• Both are **flat, non-raised** areas of colour change
• **Macule**: diameter **< 1 cm** (e.g. freckles, flat moles)
• **Patch**: diameter **> 1 cm** (e.g. vitiligo, pityriasis rosea herald patch)
cards.m: Flat lesions: small = Macule, big = Patch. You can feel neither with eyes closed.

cards.q: Papule vs plaque: how are they defined and what are classic examples?
cards.a:
• Both are **solid and raised**
• **Papule**: **< 1 cm** (e.g. acne, warts)
• **Plaque**: **> 1 cm**, **flat-topped** (e.g. psoriasis, eczema)
cards.m: A plaque is a plateau: raised, wide and flat on top.

cards.q: What is a pustule and which conditions typically produce it?
cards.a:
• Small, raised, **pus-filled** lesion with white/yellow centre on red, inflamed skin
• Examples: **acne vulgaris**, **folliculitis**
• Note: pus is not always infective (e.g. sterile pustules in pustular psoriasis)
cards.m: Pustule = Pus in a papule.

cards.q: Vesicle vs bulla: what is the size cut-off and give examples of each.
cards.a:
• Both are **fluid-filled blisters**
• **Vesicle**: **< 0.5 cm** (e.g. herpes simplex, chickenpox)
• **Bulla**: **> 0.5 cm** (e.g. bullous pemphigoid, burns, bullous impetigo)
cards.m: Vesicle = 'very small' blister; Bulla = 'big' blister. Cut-off 5 mm.

cards.q: Nodule vs cyst: how do they differ, with examples?
cards.a:
• **Nodule**: **solid**, raised, firm bump **> 1 cm**, often deeper (dermis/subcutis) - e.g. lipoma, dermatofibroma
• **Cyst**: **closed sac** containing fluid, pus or thick **keratin** - e.g. epidermoid cyst, milia
cards.m: Nodule = solid; Cyst = sac.

cards.q: What is a wheal and what is the key clinical feature?
cards.a:
• Raised, **itchy, temporary** dermal swelling (a **hive**)
• Individual wheals typically resolve within **24 hours**
• Examples: **urticaria**, insect bites
cards.m: Wheal = here today, gone tomorrow.

cards.q: What defines purpura, and how do you confirm it at the bedside?
cards.a:
• Purple, red or brownish-black spots that are **non-blanching** (bleeding into skin)
• Examples: **senile purpura**, ecchymoses
• Bedside: press a **glass slide** (diascopy) - purpura does not fade, erythema does
cards.m: Blood outside the vessel cannot be pushed away.

cards.q: Erosion vs ulcer: what is the key difference in depth?
cards.a:
• **Erosion**: shallow, moist/crusted sore with **partial loss of epidermis** - heals **without scarring** (e.g. ruptured herpes simplex vesicle)
• **Ulcer**: crater-like sore with **full loss of epidermis**, extending into dermis or deeper - may **scar** (e.g. diabetic foot ulcer, pressure ulcer)
cards.m: Erosion = epidermis only; Ulcer = goes under.

cards.q: What is a crust, and which infection is classically described by its crust?
cards.a:
• Dried **serum, blood or pus** on the skin surface (a secondary lesion)
• Examples: scab, **impetigo**
• Impetigo: **honey-coloured crusts**
cards.m: Honey crust = impetigo until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is lichenification and what causes it?
cards.a:
• **Thick, leathery** skin with **exaggerated skin markings**
• Caused by chronic **rubbing and scratching**
• Examples: **lichen simplex chronicus**, chronic eczema
cards.m: Like tree bark lichen: rough and thick from years of scratching.

cards.q: Which secondary lesion results from chronic topical steroid misuse, and what does it look like?
cards.a:
• **Atrophy**: thinning of the skin layers
• Shiny, thin, wrinkled skin with visible vessels (telangiectasia)
• Other examples: **striae**
• Hence avoid potent steroids on face, flexures and thin skin
cards.m: Steroid skin = cigarette-paper skin.

cards.q: Excoriation vs fissure: what is each and give a typical example?
cards.a:
• **Excoriation**: linear or hollowed-out **scratch** abrasion with loss of part/all of epidermis - e.g. **scabies**, scratch marks
• **Fissure**: **linear crack** that often extends into the **dermis** - e.g. **athlete's foot**, chronic hand eczema
cards.m: Excoriation = you did it (scratching); fissure = skin split itself.

cards.q: Folliculitis: features, usual organism and first-line treatment?
cards.a:
• Small, erythematous, pruritic **papules with central pustules** at hair follicles
• Superficial infection; face, trunk, extremities
• Organism: **Staphylococcus aureus**
• Treatment: **topical antibiotic** (mupirocin, clindamycin)
cards.m: One follicle, one pustule, one cream.

cards.q: What is a furuncle and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Deeper infection of a hair follicle following **folliculitis**: a **tender subcutaneous nodule** that may drain spontaneously
• Sites: face, neck, axillae, buttocks, thighs
• Organism: **S. aureus**
• Management: **drainage** + oral **cloxacillin** or amoxicillin-clavulanate for **5-7 days**
cards.m: Furuncle = boil. Pus needs a way out first.

cards.q: What is a carbuncle and why does it need more aggressive treatment than a furuncle?
cards.a:
• **Multiple coalescent furuncles** draining pus from **multiple tracts**, extending into **subcutaneous fat**
• Painful; typically **nape of neck**, back, thighs
• Management: **surgical drainage (saucerisation)** + **IV cloxacillin for 7-10 days**
• Look for **diabetes** in any patient with a carbuncle
cards.m: Carbuncle = a car-load of boils.

cards.q: Cellulitis vs erysipelas: how do they differ clinically?
cards.a:
• **Erysipelas**: **superficial** (upper dermis), **well-demarcated, raised**, bright fiery red, shiny/peau d'orange
• **Cellulitis**: **deeper** dermis and subcutis, **poorly demarcated** erythema, painful
• Both mainly **Group A Streptococcus** (cellulitis may also be S. aureus)
cards.m: Erysipelas = Edge you can trace; cellulitis = blurred edge.

cards.q: What are the slide-recommended antibiotics for cellulitis by severity, and for erysipelas?
cards.a:
• Cellulitis - **mild**: oral **cephalexin** or cefuroxime
• **Moderate**: **IV cloxacillin**
• **Severe**: **ampicillin-sulbactam**
• Erysipelas: **penicillin** (IV or oral), as it is streptococcal
cards.m: Strep loves penicillin; staph needs cloxacillin.

cards.q: A patient has recurrent boils. What should you look for in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Diabetes mellitus** (check glucose/HbA1c) and other immunosuppression
• **Nasal S. aureus carriage** (consider decolonisation)
• Household spread, poor hygiene, obesity, skin friction
• Swab for C&S to look for **MRSA**
cards.m: Recurrent boils: check sugar, nose and household.

cards.q: Which features of a red, swollen limb suggest necrotising fasciitis rather than simple cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Pain out of proportion** to signs
• Rapid spread, systemic toxicity/**sepsis**
• Dusky/purple skin, **bullae**, skin necrosis, **crepitus**, anaesthesia over lesion
• Action: **urgent surgical referral** (emergency debridement) - do not wait for imaging
cards.m: Pain > appearance = fasciitis until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Impetigo: causative organisms, typical age and usual sites?
cards.a:
• **Group A Streptococcus**, **S. aureus**, or both
• Most common at **2-5 years**
• Around the **mouth and nose**, arms and legs
• Highly contagious; usually a **clinical diagnosis**
cards.m: Impetigo = school sores of the toddler face.

cards.q: Non-bullous vs bullous impetigo: how do they differ?
cards.a:
• **Non-bullous** (most common): vesiculopustules that rupture to leave **honey-coloured crusts**; Strep and/or Staph
• **Bullous**: flaccid bullae that leave a thin collarette; due to **S. aureus exfoliative toxin**; often in infants
cards.m: Bullous = toxin-blisters from Staph; honey crust = the usual mixed type.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for impetigo?
cards.a:
• **Age 2-5 years**
• **Close contact**: crowded settings, schools, contact sports
• **Warm, humid** weather
• **Broken skin**: cuts, insect bites, scabies
• Atopic dermatitis (children); **diabetes** (older adults)

cards.q: Impetigo is usually a clinical diagnosis. When should you send a pus/wound swab for C&S?
cards.a:
• **Recurrent** impetigo
• **Widespread or severe** presentation
• Suspected **MRSA**
• **Outbreak tracing** in preschool or daycare
cards.m: Swab when it is Recurrent, Extensive, MRSA or an Outbreak.

cards.q: What are the complications of impetigo?
cards.a:
• Rare overall
• **Cellulitis**; **post-inflammatory pigmentation**
• **Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)**
• **Ecthyma** (deeper ulcerating form) with scarring
• Note: slide lists rheumatic fever; classic teaching is that ARF follows streptococcal **pharyngitis**, while skin strep mainly causes **PSGN**
cards.m: Skin strep hits the kidney; throat strep hits the heart.

cards.q: Localised vs widespread impetigo: how do you choose topical vs oral antibiotics?
cards.a:
• **Localised, few lesions**: **topical** fusidic acid 2% or mupirocin 2%, usually 5-7 days
• **Widespread**, bullous, systemically unwell or failed topical: **oral** cloxacillin or cephalexin (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic)
• Plus crust removal and hygiene
cards.m: A few spots = cream; many spots = capsules.

cards.q: What non-pharmacological measures are advised in impetigo?
cards.a:
• **Crust care**: gentle cleansing with warm soapy water or antiseptic wash (povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine) **before** topical antibiotic
• **Trim fingernails** short
• Keep lesions **covered**
• Wash clothes and bedding **daily**; do not share towels
cards.m: Soak, scrape, smear: loosen crusts so the cream can reach the bacteria.

cards.q: When can a child with impetigo return to school or nursery?
cards.a:
• When lesions have **crusted over and healed**, OR
• **48 hours after starting antibiotic** treatment
• Advise not to share towels, flannels or toys meanwhile
cards.m: 48 hours of antibiotics = back to class.

cards.q: How does PSGN after impetigo typically present, and when?
cards.a:
• Latent period after **skin** infection about **3-6 weeks** (vs 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis)
• **Cola-coloured urine/haematuria**, periorbital **oedema**, **hypertension**, oliguria
• Low **C3**; raised ASO/anti-DNase B
• Check BP and **urine dipstick** if a child develops puffiness after impetigo
cards.m: Puffy face + cola urine weeks after sores = PSGN.

cards.q: What causes leprosy and which tissues does it affect?
cards.a:
• **Mycobacterium leprae** (acid-fast bacillus), chronic infection
• Affects **skin** and **peripheral nerves**
• Also **eyes**, upper respiratory tract (**nasal mucosa**) and **testes**
• Prefers cooler body areas
cards.m: Leprosy = skin + nerves; the bacillus likes it cool.

cards.q: How is leprosy transmitted?
cards.a:
• **Droplets** from the nose and mouth of untreated patients (airborne)
• Requires **prolonged close contact** (household)
• Long incubation (average about **3-5 years**)
• Becomes non-infectious soon after starting MDT; **notifiable** in Malaysia
cards.m: Slow bug, long incubation, close contacts.

cards.q: What are the WHO cardinal signs for diagnosing leprosy?
cards.a:
Diagnose if **at least one** is present:
• **Definite loss of sensation** in a pale (**hypopigmented**) or reddish skin patch
• **Thickened/enlarged peripheral nerve** with sensory impairment
• **Acid-fast bacilli** on **slit-skin smear**
cards.m: Patch that cannot feel, nerve you can feel, bug you can see.

cards.q: How is a slit-skin smear performed?
cards.a:
• **Pinch** the skin between thumb and index finger to blanch it
• Make a small slit and **scrape tissue fluid**
• **Smear** on a slide and **heat-fix** over a flame
• Stain with **Ziehl-Neelsen** for AFB
• Usual sites: **earlobes**, forehead/eyebrows, edge of active lesions
cards.m: Pinch, slit, scrape, smear, fix.

cards.q: Which stain shows M. leprae, and what are the alternative diagnostic tests?
cards.a:
• **Ziehl-Neelsen** stain: red acid-fast bacilli
• Alternatives: **skin biopsy** (granulomas, nerve involvement)
• **PCR** for M. leprae DNA
• A negative smear does **not** exclude leprosy (paucibacillary disease)
cards.m: ZN: red rods = acid-fast.

cards.q: What is the Ridley-Jopling classification of leprosy based on?
cards.a:
• Based on the host **cell-mediated immunity** (immunity-based)
• Spectrum: **TT** (tuberculoid) - **BT** - **BB** - **BL** - **LL** (lepromatous)
• Strong immunity = few lesions, few bacilli (TT)
• Weak immunity = many lesions, many bacilli (LL)
cards.m: Tuberculoid = Tough immunity; Lepromatous = Lots of bacilli.

cards.q: Tuberculoid vs lepromatous leprosy: contrast the clinical picture.
cards.a:
• **Tuberculoid**: 1 or few, well-defined, **anaesthetic hypopigmented** plaques; early asymmetrical nerve thickening; smear **negative**
• **Lepromatous**: **many symmetrical** ill-defined macules, papules, nodules; **leonine facies**, loss of eyebrows (madarosis), nasal collapse; smear strongly **positive**
cards.m: TT = Tidy and Tough; LL = Lots and Lots.

cards.q: How does the WHO classify leprosy for treatment (PB vs MB)?
cards.a:
• **Paucibacillary (PB)**: **1-5 skin lesions**, no nerve involvement and **negative smear**
• **Multibacillary (MB)**: **> 5 lesions**, OR **nerve involvement**, OR **positive slit-skin smear** (regardless of lesion count)
• If in doubt, treat as **MB**
cards.m: Five fingers: up to 5 = PB; any positive smear = MB.

cards.q: What is the WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen for leprosy?
cards.a:
• Same 3 drugs for all (WHO 2018): **rifampicin** 600 mg **monthly** + **clofazimine** 300 mg monthly and 50 mg daily + **dapsone** 100 mg daily
• **PB: 6 months**
• **MB: 12 months**
• Warn: rifampicin red urine, clofazimine **skin darkening**
cards.m: PB = 6, MB = 12 (Multi = more months).

cards.q: What are the complications of leprosy by body region?
cards.a:
• **Face**: loss of eyebrows, **flattened nasal bridge**
• **Hands**: wasting of small muscles, weakness, loss of sensation, **claw hand**
• **Legs**: **ulcers** (plantar), foot drop
• **Eyes**: **blindness** (lagophthalmos, corneal anaesthesia)
cards.m: Leprosy disability = Eyes, Hands, Feet.

cards.q: Why do leprosy patients develop hand deformity and plantar ulcers?
cards.a:
• M. leprae damages **peripheral nerves** (sensory, motor, autonomic)
• **Sensory loss** → unnoticed burns and trauma → ulcers, secondary infection, loss of digits
• **Motor loss** → small-muscle wasting, **claw hand**, foot drop
• **Autonomic loss** → dry, cracked skin
• Prevention: daily self-inspection, protective footwear, soaking and oiling
cards.m: Leprosy does not make fingers fall off; painless injuries do.

cards.q: Which peripheral nerves should you palpate for thickening in suspected leprosy?
cards.a:
• **Ulnar** nerve (at the elbow) - most commonly involved
• **Common peroneal** nerve (neck of fibula)
• **Great auricular** nerve (neck)
• **Posterior tibial** nerve (behind medial malleolus)
• Radial cutaneous and median nerves
• Also test sensation in patches with a wisp of cotton
cards.m: U-P-G-T: Ulnar, Peroneal, Great auricular, Tibial.

cards.q: What are leprosy reactions and how are they managed initially?
cards.a:
• **Type 1 (reversal) reaction**: borderline disease; existing lesions become red, swollen; **acute neuritis** (risk of permanent nerve damage)
• **Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL)**: BL/LL; crops of tender nodules, fever, arthralgia, iritis, orchitis
• Both: **continue MDT**; **oral prednisolone** for neuritis; **refer** to dermatology/leprosy team
cards.m: Reaction ≠ treatment failure: keep MDT going.

cards.q: After diagnosing leprosy in a KK, what public health steps follow?
cards.a:
• **Notify** (leprosy is a notifiable disease in Malaysia)
• **Examine household and close contacts** for patches and thickened nerves
• Health education: curable, free MDT, non-infectious soon after starting treatment, reduce stigma
• Ensure **adherence** to the full MDT course and disability (eye, hand, foot) care
cards.m: Treat the patient, check the household, fight the stigma.

cards.q: HSV-1 vs HSV-2: which diseases does each typically cause?
cards.a:
• **HSV-1**: oral herpes (**cold sores**), **herpetic whitlow**; now the **most common cause of primary genital herpes**
• **HSV-2**: genital herpes; more likely to cause **recurrent** anogenital ulcers
• Both: painful vesicles that break and crust
cards.m: HSV-1 starts above the belt but now goes below; HSV-2 keeps coming back below.

cards.q: How is HSV transmitted and what is its incubation period?
cards.a:
• **Skin-to-skin** or mucosal contact; highly contagious
• Spread possible during **asymptomatic viral shedding**
• Incubation **2-14 days**
• Virus stays **latent in sensory ganglia** and reactivates

cards.q: What are the risk factors for genital herpes?
cards.a:
• **Unprotected** sexual activity
• **Multiple** sexual partners
• **Early sexual debut**
• History of **other STIs**
• **Immunosuppression** or stress (also triggers recurrences)

cards.q: How does a first (primary) episode of genital herpes differ from a recurrence?
cards.a:
• **Primary**: more severe, **bilateral** multiple painful ulcers, **fever, malaise**, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, **dysuria**/urinary retention; lasts 2-3 weeks
• **Recurrent**: milder, unilateral, preceded by **prodromal tingling**, heals in 5-10 days
• Stages: prodrome → vesicle → ulcer → crust → healing
cards.m: First time = flu plus ulcers; recurrence = tingle then a few blisters.

cards.q: What is the investigation of choice for suspected genital herpes and what else should you offer?
cards.a:
• **HSV PCR** (NAAT) of a swab from the **base of a fresh vesicle/ulcer** - most sensitive; allows typing
• Viral culture is an alternative; **Tzanck smear** (multinucleated giant cells) is non-specific
• Offer a full **STI screen**: syphilis serology, **HIV**, gonorrhoea/chlamydia
cards.m: Unroof the blister, swab the base.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a first episode of genital herpes?
cards.a:
• Start ideally within **5 days** of onset or while new lesions are forming
• **Aciclovir 400 mg PO 8-hourly for 7-10 days**, OR
• **Valaciclovir 1 g PO 12-hourly for 7-10 days**
• Note: slide states valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly for 2 days; the correct first-episode regimen is 1 g **twice daily for 7-10 days**
cards.m: First episode = full course (7-10 days), never 2 days.

cards.q: What is the short-course episodic treatment for recurrent genital herpes?
cards.a:
• **Aciclovir 800 mg PO 8-hourly for 2 days**
• Start at the **prodrome** or within 24 h of lesions for best effect
• Plus supportive care and avoid sexual contact while lesions are present
cards.m: Recurrence: high dose, short course, start early.

cards.q: What supportive advice is given in genital herpes, and why avoid topical antivirals alone?
cards.a:
• **Warm saline sitz baths**, analgesia, topical anaesthetic
• Maintain hygiene; **avoid skin contact/sex** during lesions; use condoms
• **Topical antivirals alone** are not recommended: little benefit and risk of **resistance**
• Counsel on recurrences and asymptomatic shedding

cards.q: When is suppressive antiviral therapy offered for genital herpes?
cards.a:
• Frequent recurrences (commonly **≥ 6 per year**) or severe psychological impact
• **Aciclovir 400 mg PO twice daily**, review after about 6-12 months
• Reduces recurrences and transmission to partners
• In pregnancy: specialist care; primary infection near term may need **caesarean section** (neonatal herpes risk)
cards.m: Six a year, suppress all year.

cards.q: What is HPV and how are low-risk and high-risk types distinguished?
cards.a:
• Non-enveloped **dsDNA** virus (family **Papillomaviridae**; slide uses the old name Papovaviridae)
• **Low-risk 6 and 11**: **genital warts** (condylomata acuminata), recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
• **High-risk 16, 18**, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58: integrate into host DNA → dysplasia → **cervical**, anal, penile, vulval, vaginal, **oropharyngeal cancer**
cards.m: 6 and 11 make warts; 16 and 18 make cancer.

cards.q: How is HPV transmitted?
cards.a:
• **Sexual skin-to-skin contact**: vaginal, anal or oral sex
• Penetrative **or non-penetrative** contact (so condoms protect only partly)
• **Perinatally** from mother to infant (can cause respiratory papillomatosis)

cards.q: How are anogenital warts diagnosed and when is biopsy indicated?
cards.a:
• Usually **visual inspection**; mostly asymptomatic lumps, may itch, burn or bleed; psychological distress
• **Biopsy** if: **atypical** lesion, diagnostic uncertainty, **not responding** to therapy, to rule out **malignancy**, and all suspected **cervical** lesions
• Cervical cytology for women
cards.m: Biopsy the odd, the stubborn and the cervix.

cards.q: What are the main treatment options for anogenital warts and which are safe in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• Patient-applied: **podophyllotoxin 0.5%** (**contraindicated in pregnancy**), **imiquimod 5%** cream
• Clinic-based: **cryotherapy**, **trichloroacetic acid (TCA)**, excision, electrocautery
• In **pregnancy**: cryotherapy or TCA
• Warts may recur; treatment does not eliminate the virus
cards.m: Pregnant? Freeze or acid - never podophyllin.

cards.q: What are the preventive measures against HPV infection?
cards.a:
• **Abstinence** (most reliable)
• **Condoms** (partial protection)
• **HPV vaccination** - offered regardless of history of warts, abnormal Pap smear/HPV test or precancerous lesions
• Continue routine **cervical screening** (Pap smear every **3 years** after normal results, or HPV DNA testing)

cards.q: What follow-up and partner management is advised for a patient with genital warts?
cards.a:
• **Follow-up within 3 months** of therapy
• **Current partner**: examine for warts, offer **testing for other STIs**, patient should inform them
• **Previous partners**: tracing is **NOT recommended**
cards.m: Current partner yes, past partners no.

cards.q: Which HPV vaccines are registered in Malaysia and which types do they cover?
cards.a:
• **Cervarix** (bivalent): HPV **16, 18**
• **Gardasil 4**: HPV **6, 11, 16, 18**
• **Gardasil 9**: HPV **6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58**
• Only vaccines containing **6 and 11** protect against genital warts
cards.m: Cervarix covers the Cervix only; Gardasil also Guards against warts.

cards.q: What is the HPV vaccine schedule under Malaysia's National Immunisation Programme and for older starters?
cards.a:
• NIP: girls aged **13 years** (Form 1), **2 doses**, second dose **6 months** after the first
• Starting at **≥ 15 years**: **3 doses** at **0, 1-2 and 6 months**
• **Immunocompromised**: 3 doses regardless of age
cards.m: Under 15 = two shots; 15 and over = three.

cards.q: What key counselling points apply to HPV vaccination?
cards.a:
• It is **preventive, not therapeutic** (does not treat existing warts/lesions)
• Can be given during **breastfeeding**
• **Cervical screening is still required**
• Contraindicated/deferred in **pregnancy** and after **anaphylaxis** to a previous dose or component

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of herpes zoster?
cards.a:
• **Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV)** after earlier chickenpox
• VZV lies **latent in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia**
• On reactivation it travels along the **sensory nerve** to the skin → dermatomal rash
• Triggered by waning cell-mediated immunity
cards.m: Chickenpox never leaves; it hides in the ganglion.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for herpes zoster?
cards.a:
• **Age > 60 years**
• Underlying malignancy (**leukaemia, lymphoma**)
• Cell-mediated immune defects (**HIV**) - zoster in a young adult should prompt an **HIV test**
• **Chemotherapy**, immunosuppressants (**steroids**)

cards.q: Describe the typical clinical course of herpes zoster.
cards.a:
• **Prodrome 1-5 days**: burning or sharp **pain along the dermatome** before any rash
• **Painful grouped vesicles** in a **unilateral dermatomal** band, not crossing the midline
• Crusting and scab separation after **10-14 days**
• Regional lymphadenopathy; thoracic dermatomes most common
cards.m: Pain first, belt of blisters second, stops at the midline.

cards.q: What are the red flags in a patient with herpes zoster?
cards.a:
• **Neurological** symptoms: headache, confusion, seizures (encephalitis)
• **Widespread rash** → disseminated zoster
• **Haemorrhagic** vesicles or purpura
• **Immunocompromised** patient; **pregnant** woman
• **Eye** involvement; **ear** involvement
cards.m: Brain, spread, blood, weak immunity, pregnancy, eye, ear.

cards.q: What is the antiviral treatment for herpes zoster in an immunocompetent adult?
cards.a:
• Start ideally **within 48-72 hours** of rash onset
• **Aciclovir 800 mg PO 5 times daily for 7 days**
• **Regular analgesia** (e.g. NSAID)
• Add a **TCA** (e.g. amitriptyline) if pain persists at about 1 week
• Still treat after 72 h if new vesicles, eye involvement, immunocompromised or elderly
cards.m: 800 mg x 5 a day x 7 days.

cards.q: How is herpes zoster treated in an immunocompromised patient?
cards.a:
• **IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 7 days**
• Switch to **oral** once improving
• Regular analgesia; TCA at 1 week if needed
• Usually requires **admission/referral** (risk of dissemination)

cards.q: Which wet dressings are used for vesiculating zoster, and where?
cards.a:
• Purpose: dry and soothe blisters, reduce **secondary bacterial infection**
• **Trunk and limbs**: **potassium permanganate 1:10,000** wet dressings
• **Head and neck**: **normal saline** wet dressings
• Apply for **20 min, 2-3 times a day**
cards.m: Purple (permanganate) for the body, plain saline for the face.

cards.q: What is Hutchinson's sign and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• Vesicles on the **tip, side or root of the nose** (nasociliary branch of V1)
• Strongly predicts **ocular involvement** in herpes zoster ophthalmicus
• Action: start oral aciclovir and arrange **urgent same-day ophthalmology referral** (keratitis, uveitis, vision loss)
cards.m: Nose tip blisters = the eye is next.

cards.q: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?
cards.a:
• VZV reactivation in the **geniculate ganglion** (facial nerve, CN VII)
• Triad: **ipsilateral facial palsy** + **ear pain** + **vesicles in ear canal/auricle** (or palate)
• May cause tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss
• Treat early with antiviral ± oral prednisolone; **refer to ENT**; worse prognosis than Bell's palsy
cards.m: Bell's palsy plus blisters in the ear = Ramsay Hunt.

cards.q: What is post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Pain persisting **≥ 3 months (90 days)** after rash onset in the dermatome
• Main risk factor: **older age**; also severe acute pain, extensive rash, ophthalmic zoster
• Early antiviral treatment reduces acute pain
• Treat with **amitriptyline**, gabapentin/pregabalin, or topical lidocaine/capsaicin
cards.m: PHN = pain that outstays the rash.

cards.q: Is a patient with shingles infectious, and to whom?
cards.a:
• Fluid from vesicles can transmit VZV and cause **chickenpox** (not shingles) in **non-immune** people
• Infectious until **all lesions have crusted**
• Keep lesions **covered**; avoid contact with **pregnant women** without varicella immunity, **neonates** and the **immunocompromised**
cards.m: Shingles gives others chickenpox, not shingles.

cards.q: Which vaccine prevents herpes zoster and who should receive it?
cards.a:
• **Recombinant zoster vaccine** (Shingrix): non-live, **2 doses** 2-6 months apart
• Recommended for adults **≥ 50 years** and immunocompromised adults (≥ 18 years)
• Reduces zoster and **post-herpetic neuralgia**
• Available in Malaysia mainly in the private sector

cards.q: What are the three important groups of superficial fungal skin infections?
cards.a:
• **Dermatophytosis (tinea)**
• **Candidiasis** (Candida spp.)
• **Pityriasis versicolor** (Malassezia)
cards.m: T-C-P: Tinea, Candida, Pityriasis.

cards.q: Which organisms cause tinea and why do they infect skin, hair and nails?
cards.a:
• Dermatophytes: **Trichophyton**, **Microsporum**, **Epidermophyton**
• They **feed on keratin** → infect stratum corneum, **hair** and **nails**
• They do not invade living tissue (hence superficial)
cards.m: Dermatophytes are keratin-eaters: skin, hair, nail.

cards.q: Name the types of tinea by body site.
cards.a:
• **Capitis**: scalp
• **Corporis**: body
• **Cruris**: groin
• **Pedis**: feet (athlete's foot)
• **Unguium**: nails (onychomycosis)
• **Manuum**: hands

cards.q: How do you tell tinea, candidiasis and pityriasis versicolor apart by appearance?
cards.a:
• **Tinea**: **annular** plaque, raised **scaly well-defined border**, **central clearing**
• **Candidiasis**: **bright/beefy-red** moist plaque in folds, less defined edge, **satellite papules/pustules**
• **Pityriasis versicolor**: multiple **light or dark patches** with **fine scale** on back/chest
cards.m: Ring = tinea; beefy + satellites = Candida; spots that change colour = versicolor.

cards.q: Where does cutaneous candidiasis typically occur and who is at risk?
cards.a:
• **Moist skin folds**: groin, axilla, **inframammary**, intergluteal, abdominal folds; nappy area
• Risk: **diabetes**, obesity, heat and sweating, antibiotics, steroids, immunosuppression
• Treat with topical imidazole and keep folds **dry**

cards.q: Pityriasis versicolor: cause, distribution and treatment?
cards.a:
• **Malassezia** yeast (normal skin flora overgrowing in heat and humidity)
• **Upper chest, back, shoulders, neck**: hypo- or hyperpigmented patches with **fine scale**
• Treat: **ketoconazole 2% shampoo** or selenium sulphide applied to the skin, or topical azole; oral azole if extensive
• Warn: **colour takes months to return** after cure; recurrence common
cards.m: Versicolor = versatile colour; the scale goes fast, the colour returns slowly.

cards.q: Tinea pedis: who gets it and how does it present?
cards.a:
• Dermatophyte infection of the feet, especially **interdigital spaces** (4th web) and soles
• Risk: **sweaty feet** in tight, occlusive shoes; communal showers
• Itchy scaly rash, **cracking/maceration between toes**, flaky peeling skin
• Portal of entry for **cellulitis** - check toe webs in leg cellulitis
cards.m: Athlete's foot: sweaty shoes, soggy toe webs.

cards.q: What is the topical treatment for tinea pedis, corporis and manuum, and for how long?
cards.a:
• Topical **imidazole** or **allylamine** cream/lotion
• e.g. **clotrimazole 1%** applied **12-hourly**
• Continue **until clinical clearance plus an additional 2 weeks** (to prevent relapse)
• Oral antifungal if extensive, nail involvement or failed topical
cards.m: Clear + 2 weeks.

cards.q: How does tinea capitis present and how does it spread?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **scalp and hair shafts/follicles**, mainly children
• Itchy scaly patches with **bald patches**; hair breaks at the scalp → **black dot** appearance
• May form a boggy inflamed mass (**kerion**) with lymphadenopathy
• Spread by contact with infected people, **animals**, or shared **combs, hats**
cards.m: Scaly bald patch in a child = tinea capitis until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Why does tinea capitis need systemic treatment, and what regimen is used?
cards.a:
• The fungus lives **inside the hair shaft/follicle**, where creams cannot reach → **topical alone is inadequate**
• **Griseofulvin** (adult 500 mg PO 12-hourly; child about 10-20 mg/kg/day) for **6-12 weeks** or until cultures negative; take with fatty food
• Adjunct: **ketoconazole 2% shampoo** 2-3 times/week for 2 weeks to reduce spore shedding
cards.m: Hair = oral; skin = cream.

cards.q: What are the features of tinea corporis?
cards.a:
• On **glabrous (non-hairy)** skin of trunk, limbs, neck and face (beard area excluded - that is tinea barbae)
• Itchy, red, **scaly advancing edge** with central clearing
• May be **nummular** with small papules or pustules at the edge
• Often from pets, other people or the patient's own feet/groin
cards.m: Ringworm: no worm, just a fungus with a raised edge.

cards.q: What is characteristic about tinea manuum?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **palms and interdigital areas**
• **Diffuse dry scaling** of the palm, usually **unilateral or asymmetric**
• Commonly coexists with **tinea pedis** (the primary source): **two feet, one hand** syndrome
• Infected nails become brittle, thick, dull and distorted
cards.m: Two feet, one hand.

cards.q: How do you confirm a suspected dermatophyte infection in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Skin scrapings** from the active edge (or plucked hair / nail clippings)
• **10-20% KOH microscopy**: branching **septate hyphae**
• **Fungal culture** for species (slow, 2-4 weeks) - needed before long oral courses (e.g. nails)
• **Wood's lamp**: some Microsporum fluoresce green; pityriasis versicolor yellow-green
cards.m: Scrape the edge, KOH shows the hyphae.

cards.q: What is tinea incognito?
cards.a:
• Tinea **modified by topical corticosteroid** use (often a steroid-antifungal combination cream)
• Steroid suppresses inflammation → loses typical ring and scale; becomes **extensive, ill-defined**, pustular
• Diagnose with **KOH scraping**; stop the steroid and use antifungal
• Lesson: do not put steroid on an undiagnosed red scaly rash
cards.m: Steroid on a fungus = the fungus goes undercover.

cards.q: What causes scabies and how is it transmitted?
cards.a:
• The mite **Sarcoptes scabiei** burrowing in the epidermis
• **Prolonged skin-to-skin contact** (households, institutions, sexual partners)
• Less commonly via shared **clothing or bedding**
• Itch is a **hypersensitivity** reaction: first infestation itch starts after 2-6 weeks

cards.q: What are the typical symptoms and sites of classical scabies in older children and adults?
cards.a:
• **Intense itch, worse at night**; often other household members itchy too
• Generalised itchy rash with small red **papules or vesicles**, excoriations
• Sites: **finger webs**, wrists, toes, buttocks, **genitalia** (penile/scrotal nodules), axillae, areolae
• Head and face usually spared in adults
cards.m: Night itch + finger webs + itchy family = scabies.

cards.q: How does scabies differ in infants?
cards.a:
• Involves the **scalp, face, palms and soles** (spared in adults)
• May show **vesicles/pustules** on palms and soles, nodules in axillae
• Hence **treat the head, face and neck** in babies and young children
cards.m: Babies get it head to toe, so treat head to toe.

cards.q: What is a scabies burrow and where do you look for it?
cards.a:
• A **thin, irregular, thread-like** greyish line in the skin (a few mm long), sometimes with a dot (mite) at one end
• Sites: **finger webs**, sides of fingers, **wrists**, palms, soles, **genital area**
• Pathognomonic; mite can be confirmed by skin scraping or dermoscopy

cards.q: Classical vs crusted (Norwegian) scabies: how do they differ?
cards.a:
• **Classical**: common, otherwise healthy patient, **low mite burden** (about 10-15), very **intense itch**, papules/vesicles/excoriations
• **Crusted**: uncommon, **immunocompromised or neurologically impaired**/elderly, **huge mite numbers**, **extremely contagious**, itch **minimal or absent**, thick crusts and hyperkeratotic plaques
cards.m: Crusted: lots of mites, little itch, highly contagious.

cards.q: How is crusted scabies managed?
cards.a:
• **Refer**/admit; **isolate** with contact precautions (outbreak risk in wards and nursing homes)
• **Oral ivermectin** (200 mcg/kg, repeated doses) **plus** topical scabicide (permethrin 5%)
• Keratolytic (e.g. salicylic acid) to remove crusts; trim nails and treat under them
• Treat all contacts and decontaminate environment
cards.m: Crusted = topical plus oral ivermectin.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for classical scabies and how is it used?
cards.a:
• **Permethrin 5% cream**, left on for **8-12 hours** (overnight), then washed off
• **Repeat after 7 days** (kills newly hatched mites)
• Safe in pregnancy and infants **≥ 2 months**
• Alternatives: **benzyl benzoate 25%** emulsion (dilute for children), sulphur ointment (young infants)
cards.m: Permethrin tonight, again in a week.

cards.q: Which body area should scabicide be applied to in adults vs babies?
cards.a:
• Adults with classical scabies: **whole skin from jawline/neck downwards**; the face is not routinely treated
• **Babies and young children** (and the elderly/immunocompromised): also treat the **scalp, face, neck** (avoid eyes and mouth)
• Apply to cool, dry skin

cards.q: Which areas are commonly missed when applying scabies treatment, and what if it is washed off?
cards.a:
• Do not miss: **body folds, groin, umbilicus, external genitalia, between fingers and toes, under the nails** (especially crusted scabies)
• If washed off (e.g. hand washing) → **reapply** to that area
cards.m: Webs, folds, genitals, nails - and reapply after hand washing.

cards.q: Why must close contacts of a scabies patient be treated, and when?
cards.a:
• Contacts may be infested but **asymptomatic** (itch takes weeks to develop)
• Treat **all household and close/sexual contacts at the same time**, even without symptoms
• Otherwise **re-infestation** (ping-pong) occurs
cards.m: Treat the whole house on the same night.

cards.q: How should clothes and bedding be decontaminated in scabies?
cards.a:
• Use **fresh, clean** bedding and clothing after treatment
• Decontaminate linen, towels and clothing used in the **previous 3-4 days**
• **Hot wash (60 °C)** and hot dry, OR sun-dry, OR seal in a **plastic bag for at least 72 hours**
• Mites do not survive long off the human body
cards.m: 60 degrees or 72 hours.

cards.q: A patient's itch persists 2 weeks after correct scabies treatment. Is this treatment failure?
cards.a:
• Not necessarily: **post-scabetic itch** commonly persists **2-4 weeks** (immune reaction to dead mites)
• Manage with emollients, sedating antihistamine at night, mild topical steroid
• Suspect failure/re-infestation if **new burrows** or new lesions appear after 4 weeks, or contacts were not treated
cards.m: Dead mites still itch.

cards.q: What are the three types of human lice and how are they transmitted?
cards.a:
• **Head louse**: Pediculus humanus capitis - head-to-head contact
• **Body louse**: Pediculus humanus corporis - lives in clothing; poverty, homelessness
• **Pubic louse**: Pthirus pubis - **sexual contact**
• Blood-feeding insects; itch may take **4-6 weeks** to appear

cards.q: How do head lice present and how are they treated?
cards.a:
• Tickling/moving sensation, scalp itch, irritability, poor sleep, scratch sores
• Nits (eggs) firmly attached near the scalp
• Treat: **permethrin 1% lotion** or **malathion 1%**, **repeat after 7-10 days**
• **Fine-toothed nit comb** (wet combing)
• Pubic lice: permethrin 1% (screen for STIs); body lice: hygiene + wash clothes/bedding
cards.m: Lotion twice, comb often.

cards.q: What is atopic eczema and what drives it?
cards.a:
• **Chronic, relapsing**, itchy inflammatory skin disease, usually starting in **childhood**
• Prevalence about **20% in children**, **10% in adults**
• Causes: **genetics** (e.g. filaggrin), **impaired skin barrier**, immune dysregulation, altered skin microbiome (S. aureus)
cards.m: Leaky barrier + itchy immune system.

cards.q: Acute vs chronic atopic eczema: how do they look?
cards.a:
• **Acute**: **papulovesicular** eruption with erythema, **weeping**, oedema and excoriation
• **Chronic**: **lichenification** (thickened scaly plaques) and **xerosis** (dry skin)
cards.m: Acute = wet; chronic = thick and dry.

cards.q: How does the distribution of atopic eczema change with age?
cards.a:
• **Infants**: **cheeks/face**, scalp and **extensor** surfaces; nappy area usually spared
• **Children**: **flexures** (antecubital, popliteal fossae), wrists, ankles, neck
• **Adults**: flexures, hands, face/neck, often lichenified
cards.m: Babies on the cheeks, kids in the creases.

cards.q: What are the UK Working Party diagnostic criteria for atopic eczema (used in the Malaysian CPG)?
cards.a:
Itchy skin (or parental report of scratching) **plus ≥ 3** of:
• History of **flexural** involvement (cheeks in children < 10)
• Personal history of **asthma or hay fever** (or first-degree relative if < 4 years)
• **General dry skin** in the past year
• **Visible flexural eczema**
• **Onset before age 2** (not used if < 4 years)
• IgE, patch test, skin prick test and biopsy are **not** diagnostic
cards.m: Itch + 3 of: Flexures, Atopy, Dry, Visible, Early onset.

cards.q: What are the comorbidities of atopic eczema?
cards.a:
• **Asthma**, **allergic rhinitis**, **food allergy** (the atopic march)
• **Skin infections** (S. aureus, eczema herpeticum)
• **Contact dermatitis**
• Cardiovascular and metabolic risk
• **Psychological/psychosocial** problems: poor sleep, anxiety, depression

cards.q: What factors trigger atopic eczema flares?
cards.a:
• **Physical irritants** (wool, sweat, heat) and **chemical irritants** (soaps, detergents)
• **Aeroallergens** (house dust mite, pollen, pet dander)
• Environmental factors (humidity, temperature)
• **Food** (mainly in young children), **microbial colonisation**
• **Psychological stress**, hormones and pregnancy

cards.q: What is the foundation of atopic eczema management and what bathing advice is given?
cards.a:
• **Emollients liberally and frequently**, even when clear (the cornerstone)
• Use **soap substitutes**; avoid irritants and triggers
• Bathing: **shorter** baths/showers, **avoid extremes** (too hot or cold), pat dry and apply moisturiser immediately
• Written **eczema action plan**
cards.m: Moisturise, moisturise, moisturise.

cards.q: How do you choose topical corticosteroid potency in atopic eczema?
cards.a:
• Match potency to **severity** and **site**
• **Face, eyelids, flexures, genitals, infants**: **mild** (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) - avoid potent steroids here
• Body/limbs: moderate (e.g. diluted betamethasone valerate)
• Thick lichenified/palms/soles: potent (e.g. betamethasone valerate 0.1%) for short courses
• Use **fingertip units**; apply once or twice daily
cards.m: Thin skin, weak steroid; thick skin, strong steroid.

cards.q: What is proactive (maintenance) topical steroid therapy in atopic eczema?
cards.a:
• After control is achieved, apply a steroid to **previously affected sites 1-2 times a week**
• e.g. **fluticasone propionate 0.05% cream twice weekly**
• Reduces **flares** in frequently relapsing eczema
• Continue emollients daily
cards.m: Weekend therapy: steroid twice a week on old hot-spots.

cards.q: What are topical calcineurin inhibitors and when are they used in eczema?
cards.a:
• **Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment** (0.03% for children) or **pimecrolimus 1% cream**
• **Steroid-sparing**: do not cause skin atrophy → useful on **face, eyelids, flexures**
• Used from **2 years** of age
• Common side effect: transient **burning/stinging**; advise sun protection
cards.m: TCI = face-friendly, no thinning.

cards.q: What is wet wrap therapy?
cards.a:
• **Two layers** of tubular bandage or garments: **inner wet layer, outer dry layer**
• Applied over **moisturiser alone or with topical corticosteroid**
• Used for **severe or refractory** flares, often in children
• Cools, reduces itch and scratching, enhances absorption

cards.q: Which tools assess atopic eczema severity and quality of life?
cards.a:
• Severity: **SCORAD**, **EASI**, **IGA**, **SASSAD**, **POEM** (patient-oriented)
• Quality of life: **CDLQI** (children), **DLQI** (adults)
• Used to guide treatment step-up and referral
cards.m: SCORAD scores the disease; DLQI scores the life.

cards.q: What is eczema herpeticum and how should it be managed?
cards.a:
• Widespread **HSV** infection in eczematous skin
• **Clustered monomorphic punched-out erosions**/vesicles, rapidly worsening painful eczema, **fever**, malaise
• Dermatological **emergency**: start **aciclovir** and **refer urgently (within 24 h)**; eye involvement → ophthalmology
• Do not mistake for a bacterial flare
cards.m: Punched-out holes in eczema = herpes, not staph.

cards.q: When should a patient with atopic eczema be referred urgently vs non-urgently?
cards.a:
• **Urgent (within 24 h)**: suspected **eczema herpeticum**; severe bacterial infection needing **IV antibiotics**; acute **erythroderma > 80% BSA**
• **Non-urgent**: diagnostic uncertainty; **severe/uncontrolled** eczema (needs potent TCS, frequent infections, poor sleep); parental concern; need for education; difficult sites; psychological disturbance
cards.m: Urgent = Herpes, IV antibiotics, Erythroderma.

cards.q: What is seborrhoeic dermatitis and what causes it?
cards.a:
• **Chronic, relapsing** inflammatory dermatitis of **sebaceous-gland-rich** skin: scalp, face, upper trunk
• Linked to overgrowth of / inflammatory response to **Malassezia** yeast
• Hence treated with **antifungals** plus mild anti-inflammatories
cards.m: Seb derm = sebum + Malassezia.

cards.q: How does infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (cradle cap) present?
cards.a:
• Mainly the **scalp**: red patches with **thick, greasy, yellowish scales/crusts**
• May involve face, flexures and **nappy area**
• Baby is usually **well and not itchy**; self-limiting in months
cards.m: Cradle cap = greasy, yellow, not itchy, happy baby.

cards.q: Which sites are typically affected by seborrhoeic dermatitis in adults?
cards.a:
• **Scalp** (dandruff), **eyebrows**, **nasolabial folds**, eyelids (blepharitis), **ears**
• **Presternal chest**, upper back, body folds
• Red rash with white or yellowish greasy scale
cards.m: Where the oil is: brows, nose folds, ears, chest.

cards.q: What are the three treatment aims in seborrhoeic dermatitis?
cards.a:
• **Modulate sebum** excretion
• **Reduce Malassezia** colonisation (antifungals)
• **Suppress inflammation** (mild topical steroids for flares)

cards.q: How do you manage cradle cap in an infant?
cards.a:
• Wash regularly with **mild baby shampoo**
• Apply **vegetable/mineral oil** to soften thick scales, then **gently brush off**
• Face/body: keep dry and clean, bathe with warm water, avoid toilet soaps, **change soiled nappies often**
• Persistent: **ketoconazole 2% cream** or mild steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) short term
• Reassure: usually resolves by 6-12 months
cards.m: Oil, soften, brush.

cards.q: What is the treatment of adult seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp and face?
cards.a:
• **Scalp**: **ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly** (leave 5 min), then weekly to prevent relapse
• **Face and body**: bland soap; **ketoconazole 2% cream BD**
• Active flares: **mild topical steroid** (hydrocortisone 1% BD) short courses
cards.m: Keto for the yeast, hydrocortisone for the heat.

cards.q: How is severe seborrhoeic dermatitis treated by site, and when do you refer?
cards.a:
• Severe on **face and flexures**: **hydrocortisone 1%** (avoid potent steroid)
• Severe on **trunk**: **betamethasone 0.02-0.05%**
• **Refer to dermatologist** if not responding to treatment

cards.q: How do you tell infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis from infantile atopic eczema?
cards.a:
• **Seborrhoeic**: onset first weeks, **greasy yellow scale**, scalp and flexures/**nappy area**, **little or no itch**, infant content, resolves within months
• **Atopic eczema**: onset after 2-3 months, **itchy** (scratching, poor sleep), cheeks and extensors, **nappy area spared**, dry skin, chronic
cards.m: Seborrhoeic = greasy and happy; atopic = dry and itchy.

cards.q: Severe, extensive seborrhoeic dermatitis in an adult should make you consider which underlying conditions?
cards.a:
• **HIV infection** (sudden severe or refractory seborrhoeic dermatitis)
• **Parkinson's disease** and other neurological disorders
• Also stress, alcohol misuse
• Offer an HIV test when the history fits
cards.m: Bad seb derm: think HIV and Parkinson's.

cards.q: What is allergic contact dermatitis and what are common causes?
cards.a:
• **Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity** to an allergen in a previously sensitised person; rash may spread beyond the contact site
• Causes: **nickel** (jewellery, buckles), chromate (cement), **cosmetics**, perfume, hair dye (PPD), **rubber/latex**, glues/acrylates, nail polish, plants
• Topical medicines: **neomycin**, **benzocaine**, topical antihistamines
cards.m: Allergic needs memory (sensitisation); irritant hurts anyone.

cards.q: Irritant vs allergic contact dermatitis: how do they differ and how is allergic confirmed?
cards.a:
• **Irritant** (most common): direct damage by **acids, alkalis, detergents, soaps, oils, solvents**; anyone with enough exposure; confined to contact area (e.g. housewife's/healthcare worker's hands)
• **Allergic**: immune-mediated, only sensitised people, small amounts suffice
• Gold standard for allergic: **patch testing**
cards.m: Patch test proves allergy; irritant has no test.

cards.q: How is contact dermatitis managed?
cards.a:
• **Identify and withdraw the trigger** (most important); protective gloves
• **Bland soaps/soap substitutes** and regular **moisturisers**
• **Topical corticosteroid** cream
• **Oral prednisolone** short course for severe/extensive cases
• **Oral antibiotics** for secondary infection

cards.q: What is acne vulgaris and how common is it in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Chronic inflammatory disorder of the **pilosebaceous unit**
• **Non-inflammatory** lesions: **comedones**; **inflammatory** lesions: papules, pustules, nodules, cysts
• Peaks in adolescence and young adulthood: about **60-68%** of Malaysian adolescents and young adults

cards.q: What are the four key steps in acne pathogenesis?
cards.a:
• **Increased sebum** production (androgen-driven)
• **Altered follicular keratinisation** → comedones
• Follicular colonisation by **Cutibacterium acnes**
• **Inflammation** around the pilosebaceous unit
cards.m: Oil, Plug, Bug, Inflammation.

cards.q: Open vs closed comedones: what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Open comedone (blackhead)**: dilated follicle, dark colour from **oxidised melanin/keratin** (not dirt)
• **Closed comedone (whitehead)**: small skin-coloured papule with a closed opening; can progress to inflammatory lesions
• Both are **non-inflammatory** lesions; best treated with **topical retinoids**
cards.m: Blackheads are oxidised, not dirty.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for acne vulgaris listed in the Malaysian CPG?
cards.a:
• **Older adolescents**
• **Oily skin** type
• Female > male
• **Hirsutism** (hyperandrogenism, e.g. PCOS)
• Diet: high **dairy and sugary** products, low fibre and fish

cards.q: How is acne diagnosed and which investigations may be needed?
cards.a:
• **Clinical diagnosis**: count non-inflammatory and inflammatory lesions
• **Microbiology** if another folliculitis is suspected (S. aureus, **Gram-negative folliculitis** after long antibiotic use)
• **Endocrine tests** if hyperandrogenism suspected (**PCOS**: irregular periods, hirsutism, sudden severe acne)

cards.q: Which scale does the Malaysian acne CPG use to grade severity?
cards.a:
• **Comprehensive Acne Severity Scale (CASS)**: **0-5** (clear to very severe)
• Grades 0 clear, 1 almost clear, 2 mild, 3 moderate, **4 severe**, **5 very severe**
• **CASS 4-5** (severe/nodulocystic) → early dermatology referral
cards.m: CASS 4-5 = see a dermatologist within 2 weeks.

cards.q: What are the topical treatment options for acne and key counselling points?
cards.a:
• **Topical retinoids** (adapalene, tretinoin): comedolytic; irritation, photosensitivity; avoid in pregnancy
• **Benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**: antibacterial, **no resistance**; can **bleach** fabric/hair
• **Topical antibiotics** (clindamycin) - always with BPO
• **Azelaic acid** (safe in pregnancy)
• Counsel: improvement takes **6-8 weeks**; do not squeeze
cards.m: Retinoid unplugs, BPO kills, antibiotic never alone.

cards.q: Why should antibiotics never be used alone in acne?
cards.a:
• **C. acnes antibiotic resistance** develops with monotherapy
• Combine topical or oral antibiotics with **benzoyl peroxide** and/or a **topical retinoid**
• Avoid using topical and oral antibiotics together
• Limit oral antibiotic courses and review
cards.m: BPO is the bodyguard against resistance.

cards.q: What oral antibiotic is used for moderate to severe acne, and how?
cards.a:
• **Doxycycline** (or other tetracycline) first-line; erythromycin/azithromycin if tetracyclines contraindicated (pregnancy, < 12 years)
• Combine with topical **BPO ± retinoid**
• Review at about **12 weeks**; avoid prolonged courses (usually ≤ 3-4 months)
• Doxycycline: take upright with water, **photosensitivity**, oesophagitis
cards.m: Doxy: upright, sunscreen, short course.

cards.q: What must you know about oral isotretinoin for acne?
cards.a:
• For **severe nodulocystic** or scarring acne, or failed adequate therapy - **specialist (dermatologist) initiated**
• Highly **teratogenic**: pregnancy test and **effective contraception** before, during and for 1 month after
• Side effects: dry lips/skin, raised lipids and liver enzymes, **mood change/depression**
• Do not combine with tetracyclines (intracranial hypertension)
cards.m: Isotretinoin: pregnancy test, contraception, mood check.

cards.q: When should a patient with acne be referred, and how urgently?
cards.a:
• **Urgent**: suspected **acne fulminans** (sudden severe ulcerating acne with fever/arthralgia); **major depression or suicidal** behaviour
• **Seen early (within 2 weeks)**: severe/**nodulocystic acne (CASS 4-5)**; severe social or psychological distress
• **Non-urgent**: diagnostic uncertainty; for dermatologist services

cards.q: When is hormonal therapy used for acne in women?
cards.a:
• Women with acne plus **hyperandrogenism** (e.g. **PCOS**), premenstrual flares, or who also need **contraception**
• **Combined oral contraceptive** (e.g. containing cyproterone acetate or drospirenone) ± spironolactone (specialist)
• Takes **3-6 months** to work; combine with topical therapy
• Check COC contraindications (migraine with aura, VTE risk, smoking > 35 years)
cards.m: Hormonal acne in women: the pill can treat the pimples.

cards.q: What is psoriasis and what is its epidemiology in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Chronic **immune-mediated inflammatory** disease of **skin and joints**
• About **0.34%** of the Malaysian population annually; slightly more in **males**
• **Bimodal** onset: **30-39** and **60-69 years**
• Familial in about **25%** (PSORS1 gene)

cards.q: What are the risk factors and triggers for psoriasis?
cards.a:
• **Family history** (PSORS1)
• **Smoking**, **alcohol**, **obesity**
• **Infection**: streptococcal URTI (guttate), skin infections
• **Skin trauma** (Koebner phenomenon)
• **Stress**, depression
• Certain **drugs**
cards.m: Smoke, drink, weight, strep, trauma, stress.

cards.q: Describe the classic lesions and distribution of plaque psoriasis.
cards.a:
• **Symmetrical, well-defined**, thick **erythematous plaques** with **silvery-white scale**
• Sites: **scalp**, **extensor surfaces** (elbows, knees), trunk/lower back, **gluteal cleft**, umbilicus
• Symptoms: itch and pain
• Contrast: eczema favours flexures and is ill-defined
cards.m: Psoriasis is on the outside (extensors); eczema hides in the creases.

cards.q: What is the Auspitz sign?
cards.a:
• **Pinpoint bleeding** when psoriatic scale is removed or scratched
• Reflects **dilated capillaries** in elongated dermal papillae beneath a thin epidermis
• Supports a clinical diagnosis of psoriasis
cards.m: Auspitz = Ouch-spots of blood.

cards.q: What is the Koebner phenomenon and which conditions show it?
cards.a:
• New lesions appearing at sites of **skin trauma** (scratches, surgical scars, burns, tattoos)
• Classic in **psoriasis**; also lichen planus, vitiligo, viral warts (pseudo-Koebner), molluscum
• Advise patients to avoid skin injury and scratching
cards.m: Koebner: injure the skin, plant the plaque.

cards.q: What nail changes occur in psoriasis and why do they matter?
cards.a:
• **Nail pitting** (nail **matrix** involvement)
• **Onycholysis**, oil-drop/salmon patch, **subungual hyperkeratosis** (nail **bed**)
• Nail disease is strongly associated with **psoriatic arthritis**
• Differential: onychomycosis (send clippings)
cards.m: Pits = matrix; thick nail = bed; nails point to joints.

cards.q: Name the clinical types of psoriasis other than plaque psoriasis and their key features.
cards.a:
• **Guttate**: many small drop-like papules on trunk, often **2-3 weeks after streptococcal throat infection** in young people
• **Inverse/flexural**: smooth red plaques in folds, **little scale**
• **Pustular**: sterile pustules (localised palmoplantar or **generalised**)
• **Erythrodermic**: **> 90% BSA** erythema - emergency
• Generalised pustular and erythrodermic need **urgent referral**
cards.m: Guttate = guttae (drops) after a sore throat.

cards.q: What comorbidities are associated with psoriasis?
cards.a:
• **Cardiometabolic**: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, **diabetes**, IHD, stroke, obesity, **fatty liver**
• GI: viral hepatitis, fatty liver, cirrhosis
• **Psychiatric**: depression, anxiety
• Malignancy: lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma
• **Psoriatic arthritis**
• Screen BP, glucose, lipids, weight, mood
cards.m: Psoriasis is a systemic disease that shows on the skin.

cards.q: How is psoriasis severity assessed by body surface area?
cards.a:
• **Palm method**: patient's **one palm (with fingers and thumb) = 1% BSA**; or rule of nines
• **Mild: BSA ≤ 10%**
• **Moderate to severe: BSA > 10%**
• Other tools: **PASI**, lattice PGA
cards.m: One palm = 1%; more than 10 palms = moderate-severe.

cards.q: How is quality of life measured in psoriasis and what are the cut-offs?
cards.a:
• **DLQI** for patients **> 16 years**; **CDLQI** for children
• **Mild: DLQI ≤ 10**
• **Moderate to severe: DLQI > 10**
• A small BSA with high DLQI (e.g. face, hands, genitals) still counts as significant

cards.q: What is first-line topical therapy for psoriasis and how much should be applied?
cards.a:
• **Topical corticosteroids** (e.g. betamethasone valerate; hydrocortisone for face/folds), used with **moisturisers**
• Potency matched to severity and site
• **Fingertip unit (FTU)**: **1 FTU = 0.5 g**, covers about **2% BSA** (two adult palms)
cards.m: 1 FTU = 0.5 g = 2 palms.

cards.q: Which topical vehicle suits which site in psoriasis?
cards.a:
• **Scalp**: **gel**/solution/foam (penetrates hair)
• **Face, genitals, body folds**: **cream** (less occlusive; use low potency)
• **Palms and soles**: **ointment** (thick skin, occlusive)
cards.m: Gel for hair, cream for folds, ointment for soles.

cards.q: How are vitamin D analogues and coal tar used in psoriasis?
cards.a:
• **Calcipotriol**: monotherapy (cream, ointment) or **combined with corticosteroid** (ointment, gel, foam); combination **twice weekly up to 52 weeks** to prevent relapse
• **Tar**: anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, reduces itch; for mild-moderate disease; **not for face, genitals or folds**; stains and irritates
• Others: salicylic acid (descaling), calcineurin inhibitors, dithranol, roflumilast, tapinarof

cards.q: Why should systemic corticosteroids be avoided in psoriasis?
cards.a:
• On withdrawal they cause **rebound flare**, including **generalised pustular** or **erythrodermic** psoriasis (life-threatening)
• Psoriasis needing systemic therapy → dermatology for methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin, phototherapy or biologics
cards.m: Oral steroid in psoriasis: calm now, pustules later.

cards.q: Which drugs can trigger or worsen psoriasis?
cards.a:
• **Beta-blockers**
• **Lithium**
• **Antimalarials** (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine)
• **NSAIDs**, ACE inhibitors (less consistently)
• **Withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids**
• Review the medication list in any new or flaring psoriasis
cards.m: BLAN: Beta-blockers, Lithium, Antimalarials, NSAIDs.

cards.q: When should psoriasis be referred to dermatology or rheumatology?
cards.a:
• **Urgent dermatology**: **erythrodermic** and **generalised pustular** psoriasis
• Dermatology: diagnostic uncertainty; **> 10% BSA**; **not controlled with topicals within 12 weeks**; special sites (scalp, face, nails, hands/feet, genitals) with major impact; significant psychosocial impact
• **Rheumatology**: suspected **psoriatic arthritis** (screen with PEST: score ≥ 3)
cards.m: 10% BSA, 12 weeks, special sites, joints.

cards.q: What is SLE and who does it typically affect?
cards.a:
• **Chronic autoimmune multisystem** disorder with inflammation in many organs
• **Relapsing-remitting** course with unpredictable prognosis
• Incidence 1.4-5.4 per 100,000 worldwide; much **more common in females**, typically aged **20-50 years**
• Manifestations: mucocutaneous, musculoskeletal, neurological, renal, haematological

cards.q: What are the risk factors for SLE?
cards.a:
• **Female** sex
• **Family history**
• Atopic disease (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis)
• **Smoking**
• **Ultraviolet light**
• Medications (e.g. **HRT**); drug-induced lupus with hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid

cards.q: What are the four subtypes of cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE)?
cards.a:
• **Acute CLE** (malar rash; strongly linked to SLE)
• **Subacute CLE**
• **Intermittent CLE** (lupus tumidus)
• **Chronic CLE** (discoid lupus - the **most common** form)
cards.m: A-S-I-C: Acute, Subacute, Intermittent, Chronic.

cards.q: Describe the malar (butterfly) rash of acute cutaneous lupus.
cards.a:
• Redness and swelling over **both cheeks and nasal bridge**
• Characteristically **spares the nasolabial folds**
• **Photosensitive**, lasts hours to days, **non-scarring**
• Strongly associated with **systemic** disease
• Contrast: rosacea (papules/pustules), seborrhoeic dermatitis (involves nasolabial folds)
cards.m: Butterfly sits on the cheeks but stays out of the smile lines.

cards.q: How does generalised acute CLE on the hands differ from dermatomyositis?
cards.a:
• **Generalised acute CLE**: diffuse papular erythema on face, upper limbs, trunk; on the hands it involves skin **between the knuckles** and **spares the knuckles**
• **Dermatomyositis**: **Gottron papules over the knuckles**, heliotrope eyelids, proximal muscle weakness
cards.m: Lupus spares the knuckles; dermatomyositis sits on them.

cards.q: What are the features of subacute cutaneous lupus (SCLE)?
cards.a:
• **Psoriasiform papulosquamous** or **annular polycyclic** plaques with central clearing
• **Sun-exposed** trunk and upper limbs (face often spared)
• Heals with **dyspigmentation but no scarring**
• Associated with **anti-Ro (SSA)**; often **drug-induced** (thiazides, PPIs, terbinafine, calcium channel blockers)
cards.m: SCLE: rings in the sun, no scars, anti-Ro, check the drug chart.

cards.q: What are the features of discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)?
cards.a:
• Most common chronic CLE
• **Erythematous scaly plaques** with **follicular plugging** (**carpet-tack sign** when scale lifted)
• Sites: **scalp, ears**, cheeks, nose, lips
• Heals slowly with **scarring** and dyspigmentation; **scarring alopecia** on scalp
• Only a minority progress to SLE
cards.m: Discoid = Destroys (scars); acute and subacute do not.

cards.q: Which other chronic/intermittent CLE forms should you recognise?
cards.a:
• **Lupus tumidus** (intermittent CLE): smooth, well-defined erythematous dermal papules/plaques on sun-exposed skin; **no scarring**
• **Lupus panniculitis**: firm tender nodules; resolve leaving **dents (fat atrophy)**
• **Chilblain lupus**: painful, pruritic, hyperkeratotic fissured lesions on fingers/toes in cold; heal with atrophy

cards.q: How is cutaneous lupus investigated?
cards.a:
• **Skin biopsy**: histopathology + **direct immunofluorescence** (lupus band)
• Bloods: **FBC** (cytopenias), **renal profile**, inflammatory markers; **urinalysis** for proteinuria/haematuria
• Serology: **ANA**, **ENA** (anti-Ro in SCLE), anti-dsDNA and complement to screen for SLE
• Severity: **CLASI** score

cards.q: How is cutaneous lupus managed in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Strict photoprotection**: **SPF 50+** broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, avoid midday sun
• **Vitamin D** supplementation (because of sun avoidance)
• **Smoking cessation** (smoking worsens CLE and reduces hydroxychloroquine response)
• **Topical corticosteroids** (or calcineurin inhibitors on face)
• Refer for **hydroxychloroquine** (first-line systemic; baseline and periodic eye screening) and suspected SLE
cards.m: Sun block, stop smoking, steroid cream, then hydroxychloroquine.

cards.q: What are the classic skin manifestations of diabetes mellitus and the basic approach to them?
cards.a:
• **Acanthosis nigricans**, **acrochordons** (skin tags), **xanthelasma**, **diabetic dermopathy**, **necrobiosis lipoidica**
• Plus increased **skin infections** (boils, carbuncles, candida, cellulitis) and diabetic foot
• Basic management: **treat the DM** - glycaemic control, diet, physical activity, weight reduction

cards.q: What does acanthosis nigricans look like and where is it found?
cards.a:
• Poorly demarcated **grey-brown hyperpigmented** plaques with a **thickened velvety to warty** texture
• **Flexural/intertriginous** sites: **back of neck**, axillae, elbows, groin, palms (knuckles)
• Mostly in **T2DM**, obesity, PCOS - a visible marker of **insulin resistance**
cards.m: Velvety dark neck = insulin resistance.

cards.q: Why does hyperinsulinaemia cause acanthosis nigricans?
cards.a:
• High insulin levels activate **IGF-1 receptors** on **keratinocytes and fibroblasts**
• → cell **proliferation** → **epidermal thickening** and hyperpigmentation
• Improves with **weight loss** and better insulin sensitivity

cards.q: Which features of acanthosis nigricans suggest an underlying malignancy?
cards.a:
• **Sudden onset, rapidly spreading**, extensive lesions
• In a **non-obese, older** adult without diabetes
• **Mucosal** involvement, **tripe palms**, itch, weight loss
• Commonly **gastric adenocarcinoma** → investigate/refer urgently
cards.m: Thin, old, sudden AN = look for gastric cancer.

cards.q: What are acrochordons and why are they linked to diabetes?
cards.a:
• Soft **pedunculated** skin outgrowths (skin tags), slightly darker than skin
• Friction sites: **neck, axillae, groin**, eyelids
• Common in **obesity**; associated with **insulin resistance/increased IGF**
• Multiple skin tags → consider screening for diabetes

cards.q: What is xanthelasma palpebrarum and what should you check?
cards.a:
• Soft/semi-solid **yellow plaques** on the **eyelids** (bilateral, medial canthus)
• **Cholesterol deposits** in the dermis
• Linked to hyperlipidaemia (including familial forms) - but about half have **normal lipids**
• Check **fasting lipid profile** and glucose; assess CV risk
cards.m: Yellow eyelids: check the lipids.

cards.q: What is diabetic dermopathy?
cards.a:
• **'Shin spots'**: small **pigmented atrophic patches on the shins**
• The **most common** skin finding in diabetes
• Associated with **longer DM duration** and **microvascular complications** (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy)
• Mechanism: microangiopathy + unnoticed trauma → poor wound healing and scarring
• Harmless; often fades within **18-24 months**; no treatment needed
cards.m: Shin spots are a window to the microvessels.

cards.q: What are the features of necrobiosis lipoidica?
cards.a:
• Rare chronic **granulomatous** disease, mostly in **T1DM**
• **Shins**: starts as firm erythematous papules → **yellow-brown plaques** with **atrophic, waxy centre**, telangiectasia and red-brown border
• Can **ulcerate** (painful)
• Theories: diabetic microangiopathy, abnormal collagen, impaired neutrophil migration
cards.m: Necrobiosis = yellow, waxy, shiny shins.

cards.q: How is necrobiosis lipoidica treated and what should be avoided?
cards.a:
• **Potent topical corticosteroids** for **early** active lesions
• **Intralesional corticosteroid** into the **active borders** of established lesions
• **AVOID topical steroids on atrophic lesions** (worsens atrophy, risk of ulceration)
• Protect shins from trauma

cards.q: What is a diabetic foot and what types of diabetic foot ulcer occur?
cards.a:
• **Infection, ulceration or destruction** of foot tissue associated with **neuropathy and/or peripheral arterial disease** in DM
• Types: **neuropathic (most common)**, **ischaemic**, mixed
• Ulcers over **bony prominences** (toes, forefoot/metatarsal heads, ankles); begin as **callus and dry skin**
• Infections are usually **polymicrobial**

cards.q: Neuropathic vs ischaemic diabetic foot ulcer: how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **Neuropathic**: **painless**, on **pressure points** (plantar metatarsal heads), surrounded by **callus**, warm foot, **bounding pulses**, dry skin
• **Ischaemic**: **painful**, on toe tips/heel/foot margins, **pale/cool** foot, **absent pulses**, prolonged CRT, shiny atrophic skin, loss of hair, thickened nails
• Check ABPI when pulses are weak
cards.m: Neuropathic = warm, painless, callus; ischaemic = cold, painful, pulseless.

cards.q: How is the 10 g monofilament test used in diabetic foot screening?
cards.a:
• Tests **loss of protective sensation (LOPS)**
• Apply perpendicular until the filament **buckles**, hold about 1-2 s, at standard plantar sites (e.g. hallux, metatarsal heads); avoid callus
• Inability to feel at **any site** = **LOPS** (at-risk foot)
• Combine with vibration (128 Hz tuning fork), pulses and foot inspection
cards.m: If the filament bends and they cannot feel it, the foot is at risk.

cards.q: How often should diabetic feet be reviewed according to risk category?
cards.a:
• **Low risk** (normal sensation, palpable pulses, no deformity): **annual** screening
• **Moderate risk** (one risk factor: neuropathy, PAD or deformity): every **3-6 months**
• **High risk** (previous ulcer/amputation, or neuropathy/PAD with deformity or callus): every **1-3 months**, foot care team
• **Active ulcer/infection**: refer to multidisciplinary foot team
cards.m: Low = yearly, moderate = quarterly-ish, high = monthly-ish.

cards.q: How is pain managed in a diabetic foot ulcer?
cards.a:
• Stepwise analgesia:
• **Mild-moderate**: simple analgesics (**paracetamol**, NSAIDs - caution with renal impairment)
• **Moderate**: **weak opioids** (tramadol, dihydrocodeine)
• **Moderate-severe**: **strong opioids** (morphine)
• Remember: new pain in a previously painless neuropathic foot may signal infection or Charcot

cards.q: How are topical and systemic antimicrobials used in diabetic foot infection?
cards.a:
• **Topical**: antiseptics (**iodine dressings**) and topical antibiotics (e.g. metronidazole, gentamicin) to relieve symptoms and promote healing
• **Systemic** only for **clinically infected** ulcers; send deep tissue cultures
• **Mild** (superficial, cellulitis < 2 cm): oral, e.g. cloxacillin/cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
• **Moderate-severe**: IV broad-spectrum, e.g. **ertapenem ± vancomycin** (if MRSA risk), refer
• Note: slide lists ertapenem ± vancomycin only; it is reserved for moderate-severe infection

cards.q: What are the key components of diabetic foot ulcer wound management?
cards.a:
• **Offloading** (most important for neuropathic ulcers): **total contact cast** (non-removable), removable cast walker, therapeutic footwear/padding
• **Debridement** of slough and callus
• **Dressings**: basic contact or advanced (hydrogel, alginate, foam, hydrocolloid, silver)
• Adjuncts: negative pressure, maggot, hyperbaric oxygen
• Surgery: **revascularisation**, debridement, reconstruction; post-amputation rehabilitation
cards.m: Off-load, clean up, cover, restore blood flow.

cards.q: What advice prevents diabetic foot ulcers?
cards.a:
• **Patient education** on daily foot care and self-inspection (mirror)
• **Intensive glycaemic control** (HbA1c)
• **Appropriate footwear**: covered, breathable shoes; check inside shoes for **foreign objects** and feet for pressure/trauma before and after wearing
• **Avoid thong slippers** and shoes with a toe box too tight or too loose
• Never walk barefoot; stop smoking
cards.m: Look daily, shoe properly, control sugar.

cards.q: Which diabetic foot problems need urgent referral to specialist care?
cards.a:
• Ulceration with **fever or any sign of sepsis**
• **Critical limb ischaemia** on vascular assessment
• Suspected **deep-seated tissue or bone infection** (osteomyelitis) with or without ulceration (e.g. probe-to-bone positive)
• **Gangrene** with or without ulceration
cards.m: Sepsis, ischaemia, bone, gangrene.

cards.q: What is pretibial myxoedema and which disease is it associated with?
cards.a:
• Skin thickening from **glycosaminoglycan (GAG) accumulation** in dermis and subcutis
• A feature of **Graves' disease** (0.5-4.3% of patients)
• Graves' triad: **pretibial myxoedema + ophthalmopathy + thyroid acropachy**
• Mechanism: **TSH-receptor antibodies** and activated T cells (IL-1a, TGF-β) stimulate fibroblasts to produce GAGs
cards.m: Graves' GAGs go to the shins.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of pretibial myxoedema?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral, firm, non-pitting** plaques or nodules (often asymmetrical)
• **Peau d'orange** with prominent hair follicles; **yellowish-brown** or waxy discolouration
• **Pretibial** areas, dorsum of feet, sites of prior trauma
• Mainly cosmetic (usually non-itchy, non-painful)
• Types: non-pitting oedema, plaque, nodular, **elephantiasic**
cards.m: Orange-peel shins in a Graves' patient.

cards.q: How is pretibial myxoedema diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
• **Clinical** diagnosis; biopsy shows **mucin/GAG** deposition in dermis
• Often asymptomatic, may **resolve spontaneously** (except elephantiasic form)
• If symptomatic: **normalise thyroid function**, weight reduction, **compression stockings**, **topical corticosteroid under occlusion**, intralesional steroids
• Avoid trauma; stop smoking

cards.q: What should you describe and examine when assessing a skin lump?
cards.a:
• Describe: **number, site, shape, size, surface**, mobility, solid or cystic, position, **consistency**, special features
• Examine: **attachment** (skin vs deep), relation to structures, **colour, temperature, pulsation, reducibility, fluctuation**, and **spread** (check **regional lymph nodes**)
• Most lumps in primary care are **benign**
cards.m: Site, Size, Shape, Surface, Skin attachment, Spread.

cards.q: What is a fibroepithelial polyp (skin tag) and how is it removed?
cards.a:
• Soft, **pedunculated** benign fibroma, 1 mm-5 cm, hangs off the skin
• Neck, axillae, trunk, groin; increases with **age** and obesity
• **No malignant potential**
• Removal (cosmetic/irritation): snip with forceps/scissors, **liquid nitrogen**, or **electrocautery** of base; small tags often need no local anaesthetic

cards.q: What are the features and management of an epidermoid (so-called sebaceous) cyst?
cards.a:
• Benign cyst from the **upper hair follicle** lined by epidermis-like epithelium, filled with **keratin** (not sebum - 'sebaceous' is a misnomer)
• Firm to soft, regular, **fixed to skin**, mobile over deeper tissue, **central punctum**
• Hair-bearing sites: scalp, face, neck, trunk
• **Surgical excision** of the whole cyst wall (else recurs); if **acutely inflamed/infected** → incise and drain, excise later
cards.m: Punctum + fixed to skin = epidermoid cyst.

cards.q: How does a lipoma differ from an epidermoid cyst on examination?
cards.a:
• **Lipoma**: soft, **lobulated**, painless, **not attached to skin**, **no punctum**; edge slips under the finger (**slip sign**); subcutaneous fat tumour
• **Epidermoid cyst**: firm, **attached to skin**, **punctum**, may discharge cheesy keratin
• Lipoma red flags (possible liposarcoma): **> 5 cm**, deep to fascia, growing, painful, hard
cards.m: Lipoma slips; cyst has a hole.

cards.q: What is an implantation dermoid cyst?
cards.a:
• Cyst formed when **epidermis is implanted into the dermis by a puncture wound**
• Continued keratin production → thick-walled cyst with **white cheesy material**
• Small, tender cystic swelling, often on **fingers** (e.g. hairdressers, tailors/sewers)
• Treatment: **excision**
cards.m: Needle in, skin in, cyst forms.

cards.q: What is a mucocele?
cards.a:
• Benign **mucus-containing** cyst of a **minor salivary gland** (duct trauma, e.g. lip biting)
• Smooth, round, **bluish or yellowish** translucent swelling
• Common on the **lower lip** and buccal mucosa
• Treatment: **excision** (may resolve spontaneously)

cards.q: Keloid vs hypertrophic scar: how do they differ and how are keloids treated?
cards.a:
• **Keloid**: excess collagen that **extends beyond the original wound margin**; does not regress; common in **dark skin**, chest/shoulders/earlobes; may itch or burn
• **Hypertrophic scar**: stays **within the wound margin** and often improves with time
• Note: slide calls a keloid a hypertrophic scar - they are distinct entities
• Keloid treatment: **compression/silicone dressings**, **intralesional corticosteroid** (triamcinolone), tranilast; excision alone has high recurrence
cards.m: Keloid kicks over the line; hypertrophic stays home.

cards.q: What is molluscum contagiosum and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Poxvirus** infection, mainly children (and adults sexually or with HIV)
• Small, shiny, pink pearly **umbilicated papules**, single or in clusters
• Spread by skin contact, shared towels, scratching (autoinoculation)
• **Self-limiting** (months to about 1-2 years) → **reassurance** first
• If needed: cryotherapy (may leave white marks), curettage, laser, antiseptics (hydrogen peroxide cream, povidone-iodine)
cards.m: Molluscum = little pearls with a dimple.

cards.q: What are seborrhoeic keratoses and how are they managed?
cards.a:
• Harmless **warty 'stuck-on'** papules/plaques of skin ageing, increasing in number after **40 years**
• Well-defined border, **pitted/greasy** surface, tan to black
• Management: **reassurance**; cryotherapy for thin lesions, curettage/electrocautery, TCA peel
• Sudden eruption of many lesions (**Leser-Trélat sign**) may signal internal malignancy
cards.m: Stuck-on, warty, harmless barnacles of age.

cards.q: What is granuloma annulare?
cards.a:
• Common benign inflammatory dermal condition (possibly delayed hypersensitivity)
• Firm, skin-coloured dermal papules arranged in a **ring** ('string of pearls'), often on **hands and feet**; **no scale** (unlike tinea)
• Children and young adults; weak association with **diabetes**
• Management: reassurance (often resolves), **potent topical steroid** (min 4-6 weeks), imiquimod, cryotherapy
cards.m: Ring without scale: think granuloma annulare, not tinea.

cards.q: What is a dermatofibroma and what is its classic sign?
cards.a:
• Common benign **fibrous nodule** (benign fibrous histiocytoma), about 7-10 mm, **mainly on limbs** (legs)
• Firm, well-circumscribed, may itch; often after insect bite/minor trauma
• **Dimple sign**: lateral pinching makes it **dimple inwards**
• Usually **solitary** (slide says multiple; multiple eruptive lesions are uncommon and suggest immunosuppression)
• Management: **reassurance**; excision if requested
cards.m: Pinch and it dimples = dermatofibroma.

cards.q: What are solar (actinic) keratoses and how are they treated?
cards.a:
• **Precancerous** scaly lesions on **sun-damaged** skin - early form of **cutaneous SCC**
• **Dry, rough, adherent scale** on a flat or thickened papule/plaque; forearms, face, scalp, backs of hands
• Surgical: **cryotherapy**, curettage and cautery, excision
• Topical: **diclofenac 3% gel**, **5-fluorouracil 5% cream**, **imiquimod**
• Sun protection; refer if thick, tender, bleeding or growing (possible SCC)
cards.m: Sandpaper spot on sun-damaged skin = actinic keratosis.

cards.q: What do you need to know about common warts (verrucae)?
cards.a:
• Benign epidermal growth due to **HPV**
• Peak in **adolescence**; average incubation about **4 months**
• Many resolve spontaneously (about 25% within 6 months)
