• Treatment: **topical salicylic acid**, formaldehyde, **cryotherapy**, curettage, electrodessication; podophyllotoxin for anogenital warts
cards.m: Warts: wait, wart paint, or freeze.

cards.q: What is a keratoacanthoma and why is it excised?
cards.a:
• Common, **rapidly growing** (over a few **weeks**) dome-shaped nodule with a **central keratin-filled crater**
• Single lesion on sun-exposed skin; more common in **immunocompromised**
• **Clinically and histologically resembles well-differentiated SCC**
• Management: **excision with histology** (curettage only if diagnosis certain); on lip or ear treat as SCC
cards.m: Volcano that erupts in weeks - excise as SCC until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Which features of a skin lesion or lump are red flags for malignancy needing urgent referral?
cards.a:
• Pigmented lesion with **ABCDE** changes: Asymmetry, irregular **Border**, **Colour** variation, **Diameter > 6 mm**, **Evolving** (change in size/shape/colour)
• **Rapid growth**, **bleeding**, **ulceration** or non-healing lesion > 4-6 weeks
• Soft-tissue lump **> 5 cm**, deep to fascia, hard, fixed or growing
• Associated **lymphadenopathy**; immunosuppressed patient
• Refer urgently for excision biopsy
cards.m: Changing, bleeding, ulcerating, big or fixed = refer.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with a lesion on his forearm that appeared after an insect bite. Examination shows a tense, clear, fluid-filled blister measuring 1.2 cm, surrounded by several fluid-filled blisters of 2-3 mm.
Which term best describes the 1.2 cm lesion?
o: Vesicle
Pustule
Bulla
Wheal
Cyst
mcq.e: Blisters are classified by size: a **vesicle** is a fluid-filled blister **< 0.5 cm** and a **bulla** is **> 0.5 cm**. The small satellite lesions are vesicles, but the 1.2 cm lesion is a bulla. Fluid content (clear vs pus) and depth (epidermal vs a closed sac) separate it from pustules and cysts.
w: Wrong - a vesicle is under 0.5 cm; this describes the small surrounding blisters, not the 1.2 cm one.
Wrong - a pustule contains pus with a white or yellow centre; this blister is clear.
Correct - a clear fluid-filled blister larger than 0.5 cm is a bulla.
Wrong - a wheal is a solid, itchy, transient dermal swelling (hive), not a fluid-filled blister.
Wrong - a cyst is a closed sac lined by epithelium in the dermis or subcutis, not a superficial tense blister.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old taxi driver attends a Klinik Kesihatan with an itchy patch on the nape of his neck that he has rubbed for several years. Examination shows a well-defined area of thick, leathery skin with markedly exaggerated skin markings. There is no scale, vesicle or ulcer.
Which secondary lesion best describes this finding?
o: Lichenification from long rubbing
Atrophy from repeated steroid use
Excoriation from acute scratching
Heaped-up scale from rapid turnover
Fissuring from deep dermal cracking
mcq.e: **Lichenification** is thick, leathery skin with **exaggerated skin markings** produced by chronic rubbing and scratching, as in lichen simplex chronicus and chronic eczema. Atrophy is the opposite (thin, shiny skin), excoriations are linear scratch abrasions, and fissures are linear cracks. Breaking the itch-scratch cycle is the key to treatment.
w: Correct - thickened skin with exaggerated markings after years of rubbing is lichenification (lichen simplex chronicus).
Wrong - atrophy is thinning of the skin (shiny, wrinkled, telangiectatic), not thickening.
Wrong - excoriations are linear or hollowed-out scratch abrasions with epidermal loss.
Wrong - scale is a visible accumulation of dead keratin (e.g. psoriasis); none is present here.
Wrong - a fissure is a linear crack extending into the dermis (e.g. athlete's foot), not a thickened plaque.

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman on aspirin is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan for dark purple, irregular flat spots on the backs of both forearms. She is otherwise well. You want to decide at the bedside whether these are purpura or simply inflammatory erythema.
Which bedside manoeuvre best answers this?
o: Wood's lamp examination in a dark room
Dermoscopy of the largest lesion
Darier sign by firmly rubbing a lesion
Diascopy by pressing a glass slide on it
Nikolsky sign by lateral skin pressure
mcq.e: Purpura is bleeding into the skin and is therefore **non-blanching**. **Diascopy** (pressing a glass slide on the lesion) empties dilated vessels so erythema fades, while purpura persists. In an elderly patient on aspirin with forearm lesions this is usually benign **senile purpura**, but generalised purpura needs an FBC and coagulation screen.
w: Wrong - Wood's lamp detects pigment change and some fungal fluorescence, not blood outside vessels.
Wrong - dermoscopy assesses pigmented lesion structure; it is not the simple test for blanching.
Wrong - Darier sign (urtication on rubbing) is used for mastocytosis, not purpura.
Correct - diascopy shows whether the lesion blanches; purpura does not blanch.
Wrong - Nikolsky sign tests for epidermal shearing in blistering disease (e.g. pemphigus, SSSS).

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of fever and a painful rash on the right cheek. Temperature 38.4 °C. There is a bright red, shiny, raised plaque with a sharply demarcated, palpable edge and a peau d'orange surface. There are no vesicles.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cellulitis
Erysipelas
Allergic contact dermatitis
Herpes zoster of V2
Malar rash of lupus
mcq.e: **Erysipelas** is a superficial (upper dermis and lymphatics) infection, almost always by **Group A Streptococcus**, so it has a **raised, sharply demarcated** fiery red edge. **Cellulitis** is deeper and **poorly demarcated**. Both cause fever, but the well-defined palpable edge points to erysipelas, which is treated with **penicillin**.
w: Wrong - cellulitis involves the deeper dermis and subcutis and has a poorly demarcated edge.
Correct - a raised, sharply demarcated, shiny red plaque with fever is erysipelas (Group A Strep).
Wrong - contact dermatitis is itchy, may vesiculate and does not cause fever with a tender indurated plaque.
Wrong - zoster gives painful grouped vesicles in a dermatome, not a confluent shiny plaque.
Wrong - the lupus malar rash is bilateral, photosensitive and not acutely tender with high fever.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 10.2%) presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a 4 cm, very painful, indurated swelling on the nape of his neck. Pus is draining from several separate openings. Temperature 38.2 °C.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Warm compresses and oral cloxacillin for 5 days
Topical mupirocin and review in one week
Oral doxycycline for 6 weeks and review
Needle aspiration and oral cephalexin for 3 days
Surgical drainage and IV cloxacillin for 7-10 days
mcq.e: Multiple coalescent furuncles draining from **several tracts** into the subcutaneous fat form a **carbuncle**, typically on the nape of the neck in diabetics. The slides recommend **surgical drainage (saucerisation)** plus **IV cloxacillin for 7-10 days**. Oral cloxacillin with drainage is for a single furuncle; topical mupirocin is for folliculitis. Glycaemic control must also be addressed.
w: Wrong - warm compresses with oral antibiotics suit a simple furuncle, not a febrile multi-tract carbuncle.
Wrong - topical mupirocin is for superficial folliculitis only.
Wrong - doxycycline is used for acne, not deep staphylococcal abscesses needing drainage.
Wrong - needle aspiration does not drain a multiloculated carbuncle and 3 days of oral therapy is inadequate.
Correct - carbuncle: surgical drainage (saucerisation) plus IV cloxacillin for 7-10 days.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of a warm, tender, poorly demarcated area of redness on his left shin. He is afebrile, well and has no comorbidities. Pulse 84/min, BP 128/78 mmHg. There is scaling and maceration between his 4th and 5th toes.
What is the most appropriate treatment according to the slides?
o: IV cloxacillin after admission to the ward
Topical fusidic acid cream three times daily
IV ampicillin-sulbactam after admission
Oral cephalexin plus treatment of the toe webs
Oral metronidazole plus treatment of the toe webs
mcq.e: This is **mild cellulitis** in a well patient, so the slides recommend **oral cephalexin or cefuroxime**; IV cloxacillin is for moderate and ampicillin-sulbactam for severe disease. The macerated toe web (tinea pedis) is the **portal of entry** and should be treated with a topical antifungal to prevent recurrence. Topical antibiotics do not reach the deep dermis.
w: Wrong - IV cloxacillin is reserved for moderate cellulitis; this patient is well and afebrile.
Wrong - topical antibiotics cannot treat infection in the deep dermis and subcutis.
Wrong - ampicillin-sulbactam is the slide choice for severe cellulitis.
Correct - mild cellulitis: oral cephalexin, and treat the tinea pedis portal of entry.
Wrong - metronidazole covers anaerobes and does not cover streptococci or S. aureus.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with 4 days of three small lesions around her left nostril. They began as small blisters and are now covered with golden-yellow crusts. She is afebrile, playful and has no lymphadenopathy. There are no lesions elsewhere.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral cloxacillin for 7 days with topical steroid
Remove crusts and apply topical fusidic acid 2%
Oral aciclovir and keep the lesions covered
Topical clotrimazole 1% until clear plus 2 weeks
Topical hydrocortisone 1% and an emollient
mcq.e: Honey-crusted lesions around the nose in a preschool child are **non-bullous impetigo**. For **localised** disease in a well child, gently remove crusts (warm soapy water or antiseptic) and apply a **topical antibiotic** (fusidic acid 2% or mupirocin 2%) for 5-7 days. **Oral** antibiotics are kept for widespread, bullous or non-responding disease, and steroids worsen infection.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics are for widespread or severe impetigo, and a topical steroid would worsen infection.
Correct - localised impetigo: crust removal plus topical fusidic acid (or mupirocin) for 5-7 days.
Wrong - aciclovir treats HSV; golden crusts without grouped vesicles suggest bacterial impetigo.
Wrong - clotrimazole is an antifungal and has no role in streptococcal or staphylococcal impetigo.
Wrong - a steroid without an antibiotic suppresses defences and spreads the infection.

mcq.stem:
A kindergarten teacher brings a 5-year-old boy to a Klinik Kesihatan with crusted lesions on his face and legs. She reports that 6 other children in the same class developed similar lesions in the past 2 weeks. The boy is afebrile and well.
Which investigation is indicated?
o: Pus or wound swab for culture and sensitivity
Skin scraping from the edge for KOH microscopy
Serum antistreptolysin O titre for each child
Tzanck smear from the base of a new lesion
Full blood count and blood culture for the child
mcq.e: Impetigo is usually a **clinical diagnosis**, but the slides list indications for a **pus/wound swab for C&S**: recurrent disease, widespread or severe presentation, suspected **MRSA**, and **outbreak tracing in preschool or daycare**. Here the cluster in a kindergarten makes a swab appropriate. Serology and blood cultures do not guide treatment of uncomplicated skin infection.
w: Correct - an outbreak in a kindergarten is an indication for a swab for culture and sensitivity (including MRSA).
Wrong - KOH microscopy looks for fungal hyphae, not bacteria.
Wrong - ASO titres are not used to diagnose impetigo and would not guide outbreak control.
Wrong - a Tzanck smear looks for viral giant cells (HSV, VZV).
Wrong - a well, afebrile child with skin infection does not need blood cultures.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with puffy eyes on waking for 3 days and dark, cola-coloured urine. His mother says he had crusted sores on his legs about 3 weeks ago that healed without treatment. BP 132/88 mmHg. Urine dipstick: blood 3+, protein 1+.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Minimal change nephrotic syndrome of childhood
IgA nephropathy
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Acute rheumatic fever
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
mcq.e: **PSGN** follows a streptococcal **skin** infection after a latent period of about **3-6 weeks** (1-2 weeks after pharyngitis), with haematuria, oedema and hypertension; C3 is low. **IgA nephropathy** causes haematuria within 1-2 days of an infection. Rheumatic fever typically follows streptococcal **pharyngitis**, not impetigo.
w: Wrong - minimal change disease gives heavy proteinuria and oedema without macroscopic haematuria or hypertension.
Wrong - IgA nephropathy causes haematuria within days of an infection, not after a 3-week latent period.
Correct - haematuria, oedema and hypertension 3 weeks after impetigo indicate PSGN.
Wrong - rheumatic fever follows streptococcal pharyngitis and presents with carditis and arthritis, not nephritis.
Wrong - SSSS is a staphylococcal toxin illness with widespread skin peeling, not a renal syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 24 hours of left leg swelling after a minor cut. He has severe pain far worse than the visible redness. The skin is dusky with bullae and there is crepitus on palpation. Pulse 118/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, temperature 38.9 °C.
What is the best next step?
o: Oral cephalexin and review in 48 hours
Mark the margin and start oral cloxacillin
Arrange an outpatient Doppler ultrasound
IV cloxacillin in the KK and review tomorrow
Resuscitate and refer urgently for surgery
mcq.e: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, **bullae**, **crepitus** and shock signal **necrotising fasciitis**, a surgical emergency. Start resuscitation (IV fluids, oxygen, first antibiotic dose if available) and arrange **immediate surgical referral** for debridement. Do not delay for imaging or observe as if it were simple cellulitis.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics and delayed review are dangerous in a shocked patient with necrotising infection.
Wrong - marking the margin is useful for simple cellulitis, not for a septic patient with crepitus.
Wrong - imaging must not delay surgery; this is not suspected DVT.
Wrong - this needs emergency surgical debridement today, not KK treatment with review.
Correct - suspected necrotising fasciitis: resuscitate and refer urgently for surgical debridement.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old migrant plantation worker is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan with three hypopigmented patches on his trunk. Each patch has definite loss of sensation to a wisp of cotton. No peripheral nerve is thickened. A slit-skin smear from the earlobe shows acid-fast bacilli.
What is the correct WHO classification and MDT duration?
o: Paucibacillary leprosy - MDT for 6 months
Multibacillary leprosy - MDT for 12 months
Paucibacillary leprosy - MDT for 12 months
Multibacillary leprosy - MDT for 6 months
Multibacillary leprosy - MDT for 24 months
mcq.e: WHO classifies leprosy for treatment as **paucibacillary** (1-5 lesions, no nerve involvement, **negative smear**) or **multibacillary** (> 5 lesions, nerve involvement, **or a positive smear**). A **positive slit-skin smear makes the case MB regardless of lesion count**. MB is treated with rifampicin, clofazimine and dapsone for **12 months** (PB 6 months).
w: Wrong - three lesions alone would suggest PB, but a positive smear overrides lesion count.
Correct - a positive smear means MB, treated with 12 months of MDT.
Wrong - PB is not the right class, and PB MDT lasts 6 months, not 12.
Wrong - MB is right but its MDT lasts 12 months, not 6.
Wrong - the current WHO MB regimen is 12 months; 24 months is an outdated duration.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with a 6-month history of a hypopigmented patch on his forearm. Sensation to cotton wool is reduced within the patch and the great auricular nerve is palpably thickened. You plan a test to look for the organism and help classify the disease.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: Skin scraping from the edge for KOH microscopy
Wood's lamp examination of the patch in a dark room
Serum ANA and ENA antibody panel
Slit-skin smear with Ziehl-Neelsen stain
Patch testing with a standard allergen series
mcq.e: An anaesthetic hypopigmented patch with a thickened nerve meets the WHO cardinal signs of **leprosy**. A **slit-skin smear** (pinch, slit, scrape, heat-fix) stained with **Ziehl-Neelsen** shows acid-fast M. leprae and grades bacillary load, which helps classify PB vs MB. A negative smear does not exclude leprosy; biopsy and PCR are alternatives.
w: Wrong - KOH looks for fungal hyphae; tinea patches are scaly and not anaesthetic.
Wrong - Wood's lamp helps with vitiligo or pityriasis versicolor, not with mycobacteria.
Wrong - ANA and ENA are for lupus, which does not cause sensory loss or nerve thickening.
Correct - a slit-skin smear with ZN stain detects acid-fast bacilli and supports classification.
Wrong - patch testing investigates allergic contact dermatitis.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old fisherman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a reddish, slightly raised patch on his thigh that has been present for 8 months and does not itch. You are examining him to decide whether he meets the WHO criteria for leprosy.
Which single finding would be sufficient to diagnose leprosy?
o: Definite loss of sensation within the patch
Fine scale that scrapes off easily
Itching that is worse at night
Central clearing with an active edge
Yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp
mcq.e: WHO diagnoses leprosy when **at least one cardinal sign** is present: **definite loss of sensation in a hypopigmented or reddish patch**, a **thickened peripheral nerve** with sensory impairment, or **acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear**. Scale, central clearing and nocturnal itch point to other diagnoses such as tinea or scabies.
w: Correct - definite sensory loss in a pale or reddish patch is a WHO cardinal sign.
Wrong - fine scale suggests pityriasis versicolor or other superficial conditions.
Wrong - nocturnal itch is typical of scabies; leprosy patches are usually not itchy.
Wrong - central clearing with an active scaly edge suggests tinea corporis.
Wrong - yellow-green fluorescence suggests pityriasis versicolor or some tinea capitis species.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man is 4 months into multibacillary MDT for leprosy. He returns to a Klinik Kesihatan because his existing skin patches have become red, swollen and tender over one week. His right ulnar nerve is painful and he now has new weakness of the little finger. He is afebrile.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop MDT until the reaction settles
Switch to a different antileprosy regimen
Add oral aciclovir for 7 days
Reassure and give NSAIDs only
Continue MDT and start oral prednisolone
mcq.e: Inflamed existing lesions with **acute neuritis** during treatment is a **type 1 (reversal) reaction**, an immune flare, not drug failure. **MDT must continue**, and **oral prednisolone** is started promptly to prevent permanent nerve damage, with referral to the dermatology or leprosy team. Stopping MDT risks relapse and resistance.
w: Wrong - MDT must never be stopped for a reaction; it is an immune response, not toxicity.
Wrong - a reaction does not mean treatment failure, so the regimen does not change.
Wrong - this is not a viral infection; aciclovir has no role.
Wrong - NSAIDs alone do not protect against nerve damage from acute neuritis.
Correct - type 1 reaction with neuritis: continue MDT and give oral prednisolone, and refer.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man who completed treatment for leprosy 3 years ago presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a painless ulcer under his first metatarsal head. He did not notice it until he saw blood on his sock. Foot pulses are strong and the foot is warm.
What is the main underlying mechanism of this ulcer?
o: Peripheral arterial occlusion in the foot
Direct invasion of plantar bone by bacilli
Loss of protective sensation in the sole
Clofazimine-induced fragility of the skin
Venous hypertension from incompetent valves
mcq.e: M. leprae damages **peripheral nerves**; **sensory loss** means repeated pressure and minor trauma go unnoticed, leading to **plantar ulcers**, much like the diabetic neuropathic foot. Motor and autonomic damage add deformity and dry, cracked skin. Prevention relies on daily self-inspection, protective footwear and soaking and oiling the skin.
w: Wrong - strong pulses and a warm foot argue against ischaemia.
Wrong - the ulcer is due to unnoticed pressure, not direct bacillary invasion of bone.
Correct - sensory neuropathy causes painless pressure ulcers that go unnoticed.
Wrong - clofazimine darkens skin; it does not cause plantar ulcers.
Wrong - venous ulcers occur around the medial malleolus, not under the metatarsal heads.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with leprosy at a Klinik Kesihatan and started on MDT. She lives with her husband, two children and her elderly mother. She is worried about her family.
Which public health action should follow?
o: Notify and examine all household contacts
Isolate the patient at home for 3 months
Give BCG to the patient before starting MDT
Give all contacts a full 6-month MDT course
Repeat the slit-skin smear every month
mcq.e: Leprosy is **notifiable** in Malaysia. Household and close contacts are at highest risk and should be **examined for anaesthetic patches and thickened nerves** so new cases are found early. Patients become **non-infectious soon after starting MDT**, so isolation is not needed and stigma should be addressed. Contacts are not given full MDT unless they have disease.
w: Correct - notify the case and screen household contacts for skin patches and thickened nerves.
Wrong - patients are non-infectious soon after starting MDT; isolation adds stigma without benefit.
Wrong - BCG does not treat established leprosy and is not given before MDT.
Wrong - contacts are examined, not treated with full MDT unless they have leprosy.
Wrong - monthly smears are not needed; clinical review and adherence matter more.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of painful genital sores, fever, malaise and burning on passing urine. She has a new partner. Examination shows multiple shallow painful ulcers on both labia with tender inguinal nodes. She has never had similar lesions.
What is the most appropriate antiviral treatment?
o: Topical aciclovir cream five times daily alone
Oral aciclovir 800 mg 8-hourly for 2 days
IM benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU single dose
Oral valaciclovir 500 mg daily for one year
Oral aciclovir 400 mg 8-hourly for 7-10 days
mcq.e: A first episode of genital herpes (bilateral painful ulcers, systemic symptoms, dysuria) is treated with **aciclovir 400 mg 8-hourly for 7-10 days**, ideally within 5 days of onset. The 2-day 800 mg course is for **recurrences**, and topical antivirals alone are not recommended. Note: the slide gives valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly for 2 days; the correct first-episode regimen is 1 g twice daily for 7-10 days.
w: Wrong - topical aciclovir alone is ineffective and risks resistance.
Wrong - the 2-day 800 mg course is episodic treatment for recurrent herpes, too short for a primary episode.
Wrong - benzathine penicillin treats syphilis, whose chancre is usually single and painless.
Wrong - long-term suppression is for frequent recurrences, not a first episode.
Correct - primary genital herpes: aciclovir 400 mg 8-hourly for 7-10 days.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of painful grouped vesicles and shallow ulcers on the shaft of his penis. Some lesions are still intact. He requests confirmation of the cause before discussing it with his partner.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: Tzanck smear from the edge of a crusted ulcer
Serum HSV type-specific IgG antibody titre
HSV PCR swab from the base of a fresh ulcer
Dark-ground microscopy of the ulcer exudate
Gram stain of a urethral swab for diplococci
mcq.e: **HSV PCR (NAAT)** on a swab from the **base of a fresh vesicle or ulcer** is the most sensitive test and allows typing (HSV-1 vs HSV-2), which helps counselling on recurrence. Tzanck smears are non-specific and serology cannot date or locate an infection. Always offer a full STI screen (syphilis, HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia).
w: Wrong - Tzanck smears are insensitive, cannot distinguish HSV from VZV, and crusted lesions yield little virus.
Wrong - serology shows past exposure but cannot confirm that these lesions are herpetic.
Correct - PCR from a fresh lesion base is the investigation of choice and allows typing.
Wrong - dark-ground microscopy is for treponemes in syphilitic chancres, which are usually painless.
Wrong - Gram stain of a urethral swab investigates gonococcal urethritis, not genital ulcers.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant attends a Klinik Kesihatan antenatal clinic with several soft, skin-coloured cauliflower-like papules on the vulva that appeared over 2 months. They are not painful.
Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution applied at home
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen in clinic
Oral aciclovir 400 mg 8-hourly for 10 days
Topical 5-fluorouracil 5% cream applied daily
Imiquimod 5% cream three times a week at home
mcq.e: These are **anogenital warts** (HPV 6 and 11). In **pregnancy**, physically destructive treatment (**cryotherapy**) or trichloroacetic acid is used. **Podophyllotoxin** is antimitotic and **contraindicated in pregnancy**, and imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil are avoided because of limited safety data. Warts often grow in pregnancy and may regress after delivery.
w: Wrong - podophyllotoxin is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Correct - cryotherapy (or TCA) is the safe choice for genital warts in pregnancy.
Wrong - aciclovir treats HSV; warts are caused by HPV, which antivirals do not clear.
Wrong - 5-fluorouracil is cytotoxic and avoided in pregnancy; it is not standard wart treatment here.
Wrong - imiquimod is not recommended in pregnancy because safety data are insufficient.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old girl who was absent from school during the Form 1 vaccination programme attends a Klinik Kesihatan asking for HPV vaccination. She is healthy, not pregnant and has no allergies.
Which dosing schedule is appropriate?
o: 1 dose now with no booster needed
2 doses at 0 and 6 months
2 doses at 0 and 12 months
3 doses at 0, 1-2 and 6 months
3 doses at 0, 6 and 12 months
mcq.e: Under Malaysia's NIP, girls aged **13** receive **2 doses 6 months apart**. When vaccination starts at **15 years or older** (or in immunocompromised people), **3 doses at 0, 1-2 and 6 months** are needed because the immune response is weaker. The vaccine is preventive, and cervical screening is still needed later.
w: Wrong - the slides describe a single dose for no age group.
Wrong - the 2-dose schedule applies to those starting before age 15, such as the NIP at 13 years.
Wrong - this is not the recommended interval for any group in the slides.
Correct - starting at 15 years or older needs 3 doses at 0, 1-2 and 6 months.
Wrong - the third dose is due at 6 months, not 12 months.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her 4-month-old baby attends a Klinik Kesihatan asking for HPV vaccination. She had a Pap smear last year showing low-grade changes, which has since been followed up. She asks what the vaccine will do for her.
Which counselling statement is correct?
o: She must stop breastfeeding before she can be vaccinated
Vaccinate now and continue routine cervical screening
Vaccination will clear any existing HPV infection
Vaccination is futile after an abnormal Pap smear
Pap smears are unnecessary once fully vaccinated
mcq.e: The HPV vaccine is **preventive, not therapeutic**: it does not clear existing infection, but it protects against types she has not yet acquired, so it is offered **regardless of previous abnormal Pap smears or warts**. It **can be given during breastfeeding** (it is contraindicated in pregnancy). Because vaccines do not cover every oncogenic type, **cervical screening must continue**.
w: Wrong - HPV vaccine can be given during breastfeeding; only pregnancy is a contraindication.
Correct - she can be vaccinated now and must continue cervical screening.
Wrong - the vaccine is preventive and does not treat existing infection or lesions.
Wrong - vaccination is still offered after abnormal cytology, as it protects against other HPV types.
Wrong - screening is still needed because vaccines do not cover all oncogenic HPV types.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man is treated at a Klinik Kesihatan for cauliflower-like papules on the penile shaft. He has had a steady partner for 1 year and had four other partners in the 3 years before that. He asks whom he should tell.
What is the most appropriate advice on partner management?
o: Trace and treat all partners from the past 3 years
No partner needs to be told as warts are harmless
Current partner should start podophyllotoxin now
Inform current partner and offer them STI testing
Both must avoid sex for life to prevent spread
mcq.e: For genital warts, the **current partner** may benefit from examination for warts and should be **offered testing for other STIs**, and the patient should inform them because wart-causing HPV types are transmissible. **Tracing of previous partners is NOT recommended**. Follow-up is within 3 months of therapy.
w: Wrong - tracing previous partners is not recommended for genital warts.
Wrong - the current partner should be told, examined and offered STI testing.
Wrong - partners are treated only if warts are found; podophyllotoxin is not given blindly.
Correct - inform the current partner and offer examination and STI testing.
Wrong - lifelong abstinence is not advised; condoms and treatment reduce transmission.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with known genital herpes attends a Klinik Kesihatan. She has had 8 painful recurrences in the past year, each treated with short antiviral courses. The episodes are affecting her relationship and her work. She is not pregnant.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Suppressive oral aciclovir 400 mg twice daily
Episodic oral aciclovir 800 mg 8-hourly for 2 days
Topical aciclovir cream at each prodrome
Repeat primary course 400 mg 8-hourly for 10 days
Single dose IM benzathine penicillin
mcq.e: Frequent recurrences (commonly **6 or more per year**) or major psychological impact are indications for **suppressive therapy**, e.g. **aciclovir 400 mg twice daily**, reviewed after 6-12 months. It reduces recurrences and transmission. Episodic 2-day courses suit infrequent recurrences, and topical antivirals alone are not recommended.
w: Correct - frequent recurrences warrant daily suppressive aciclovir 400 mg twice daily.
Wrong - episodic treatment has already failed to control 8 recurrences a year.
Wrong - topical antivirals alone are ineffective and risk resistance.
Wrong - repeating a first-episode course does not prevent future recurrences.
Wrong - penicillin treats syphilis, not HSV.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of a painful rash on the right side of her chest that began after 3 days of burning pain. There are grouped vesicles on a red base in a band from the spine to the sternum that does not cross the midline. She is otherwise healthy and eGFR is normal.
What is the most appropriate antiviral regimen?
o: Oral aciclovir 400 mg 8-hourly for 7-10 days
Oral aciclovir 800 mg 8-hourly for 2 days
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 7 days
Topical aciclovir cream five times daily for 10 days
Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
mcq.e: Herpes zoster in an **immunocompetent** adult is treated with **aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days**, ideally started **within 48-72 hours** of rash onset, with regular analgesia. The 400 mg and 2-day regimens are for HSV, and IV aciclovir is for the immunocompromised. Starting early reduces acute pain and may lower the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia.
w: Wrong - 400 mg 8-hourly is the HSV first-episode dose and too low for VZV.
Wrong - 800 mg 8-hourly for 2 days is episodic treatment for recurrent HSV.
Wrong - IV aciclovir is reserved for immunocompromised or complicated zoster.
Wrong - topical aciclovir has no role in shingles.
Correct - immunocompetent zoster: oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of painful vesicles on the left side of his forehead and scalp. Vesicles are also present on the tip of his nose. His left eye is red and watering, and visual acuity is 6/12 on the left.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral aciclovir and review in the clinic in a week
Topical steroid eye drops and oral aciclovir
Oral aciclovir and urgent same-day eye referral
Analgesia only as the rash is over 48 hours old
Oral prednisolone alone and review in 3 days
mcq.e: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (**Hutchinson's sign**, nasociliary branch of V1) strongly predict **ocular involvement** in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Start oral aciclovir and arrange **same-day ophthalmology referral** because keratitis and uveitis can threaten sight. GPs should not start steroid eye drops, which can worsen viral keratitis.
w: Wrong - a red eye with reduced vision in HZO needs same-day eye assessment, not review in a week.
Wrong - steroid eye drops should only be started by an ophthalmologist after slit-lamp examination.
Correct - Hutchinson's sign with a red eye: oral aciclovir plus urgent same-day ophthalmology referral.
Wrong - eye involvement is an indication to treat even after 72 hours, and this is only 2 days.
Wrong - steroids alone without antiviral cover are inappropriate in HZO.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of severe right ear pain followed by small vesicles in the right external ear canal and on the concha. Today he cannot close his right eye or raise his right eyebrow, and the right corner of his mouth droops. He also reports tinnitus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bell's palsy
Acute otitis externa
Herpes simplex labialis
Cholesteatoma with facial nerve erosion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome
mcq.e: **Ramsay Hunt syndrome** is VZV reactivation in the **geniculate ganglion**: ipsilateral **lower motor neurone facial palsy** (forehead involved), **ear pain** and **vesicles in the ear canal or auricle**, sometimes with tinnitus, vertigo or hearing loss. It has a worse prognosis than Bell's palsy and needs early antiviral (with or without steroid) and ENT referral.
w: Wrong - Bell's palsy is idiopathic and has no vesicles in the ear.
Wrong - otitis externa causes canal pain and discharge but not facial palsy with vesicles.
Wrong - herpes labialis affects the lips and does not cause facial palsy.
Wrong - cholesteatoma causes chronic foul discharge and hearing loss, not acute vesicles.
Correct - ear pain, ear-canal vesicles and LMN facial palsy are Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a painful vesicular rash along the left T10 dermatome for 2 days. There are now also more than 20 scattered vesicles on his trunk and arms outside the dermatome. Temperature 38.1 °C.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit for IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly
Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily at home
Oral valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly for 2 days
Potassium permanganate dressings only
Oral prednisolone with oral aciclovir at home
mcq.e: Vesicles beyond the dermatome in an **immunocompromised** patient indicate **disseminated zoster**, a red flag with risk of visceral involvement (pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis). The slides recommend **IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 7 days**, switching to oral once improving, so the patient needs **admission**.
w: Correct - disseminated zoster in an immunocompromised patient needs admission for IV aciclovir.
Wrong - oral therapy at home is the regimen for uncomplicated zoster in immunocompetent adults.
Wrong - a 2-day course is HSV episodic treatment and far too short for zoster.
Wrong - dressings are supportive only and do not treat dissemination.
Wrong - steroids add immunosuppression and home oral therapy is inadequate here.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman returns to a Klinik Kesihatan 4 months after shingles in the left T8 dermatome. The rash healed with faint scars, but she still has constant burning pain in the same area, and light touch from clothing is very painful. Paracetamol has not helped.
Which medication is most appropriate?
o: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily
Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily
Amitriptyline at night, low dose
Topical betamethasone valerate 0.1%
Oral cloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly
mcq.e: Pain persisting **3 months or more** after zoster is **post-herpetic neuralgia**, a neuropathic pain with allodynia. First-line options are **low-dose amitriptyline** at night (slides: TCA from week 1 if pain persists), **gabapentin or pregabalin**, or topical lidocaine. Antivirals only help in the acute phase, and steroids do not prevent or treat PHN.
w: Wrong - antivirals reduce acute pain only when started early; they do not treat established PHN.
Wrong - corticosteroids do not treat or prevent post-herpetic neuralgia.
Correct - neuropathic pain after zoster responds to low-dose amitriptyline (or gabapentinoids).
Wrong - topical steroid treats inflammatory dermatoses, not neuropathic pain.
Wrong - there is no infection; antibiotics have no role.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man is being treated with oral aciclovir for herpes zoster of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. He returns to a Klinik Kesihatan because the vesicles on his cheek are weeping and uncomfortable. There is no sign of secondary infection and the eye is not involved.
Which wet dressing is recommended for this site?
o: Potassium permanganate 1:10,000 soaks
Povidone-iodine 10% paint twice daily
Silver sulfadiazine cream three times daily
Normal saline soaks 20 min 2-3 times daily
Calamine lotion applied every 2 hours
mcq.e: Wet dressings dry and soothe weeping vesicles and reduce secondary bacterial infection. The slides recommend **normal saline** wet dressings for the **head and neck**, and **potassium permanganate 1:10,000** for the **trunk and limbs**, each for 20 minutes 2-3 times a day. Permanganate stains and irritates, so it is avoided on the face.
w: Wrong - potassium permanganate soaks are for the trunk and limbs, not the face.
Wrong - povidone-iodine paint is an antiseptic, not the recommended soothing wet dressing.
Wrong - silver sulfadiazine is a burns cream and is not used on weeping zoster here.
Correct - normal saline wet dressings are recommended for head and neck zoster.
Wrong - calamine dries and cakes on weeping lesions and is not the slide recommendation.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with 6 weeks of itchy, scaly patches of hair loss on his scalp. Within the patches, hairs are broken off at the scalp surface, leaving black dots. The family recently adopted a kitten. There is a small tender occipital lymph node.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Clotrimazole 1% cream 12-hourly until clear plus 2 weeks
Oral griseofulvin for 6-12 weeks with ketoconazole shampoo
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo 2-3 times a week for 2 weeks only
Betamethasone scalp lotion with clotrimazole cream for 4 weeks
Oral cloxacillin for 7 days with chlorhexidine scalp wash
mcq.e: Scaly patchy alopecia with **black dots** in a child is **tinea capitis**. The fungus lives **inside the hair shaft and follicle**, so **topical treatment alone is inadequate**; give **oral griseofulvin for 6-12 weeks** (or until cultures are negative). **Ketoconazole 2% shampoo** is an adjunct that reduces spore shedding and spread to others.
w: Wrong - creams do not reach fungus inside the hair shaft; topical treatment alone fails.
Correct - tinea capitis needs oral griseofulvin plus adjunctive ketoconazole shampoo.
Wrong - shampoo alone only reduces spore shedding; it does not cure tinea capitis.
Wrong - steroids worsen fungal infection, and topical antifungals are inadequate on the scalp.
Wrong - this is a dermatophyte infection, not a bacterial one.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with a groin rash. Six weeks ago he bought a cream from a pharmacy that contained betamethasone and applied it daily. The rash initially felt better but has now spread to both thighs and the lower abdomen. It is ill-defined, with scattered pustules and very little scale.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Skin scraping for KOH microscopy
Switch to a more potent topical steroid
Patch testing for contact allergens
Skin biopsy for histopathology
Swab for bacterial culture
mcq.e: A groin rash that spreads and loses its typical ring after topical steroid use suggests **tinea incognito**: the steroid suppresses inflammation and scale while the dermatophyte flourishes. Confirm with **skin scrapings for KOH microscopy** (septate hyphae), stop the steroid and start an antifungal. The lesson is never to apply steroids to an undiagnosed red scaly rash.
w: Correct - suspected tinea incognito is confirmed quickly with KOH microscopy of scrapings.
Wrong - a stronger steroid would worsen a steroid-modified fungal infection.
Wrong - patch testing is for allergic contact dermatitis, which this history does not suggest.
Wrong - biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when simple KOH microscopy can confirm the diagnosis.
Wrong - pustules here are follicular fungal lesions; a bacterial swab will not identify the cause.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old construction worker attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 months of pale patches on his upper back, chest and shoulders. The patches are mildly itchy and became more noticeable after he got a tan. Gentle scraping produces a fine, powdery scale. Sensation within the patches is normal.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Topical hydrocortisone 1% twice daily
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied to the skin
Oral griseofulvin 500 mg 12-hourly for 6 weeks
Oral doxycycline 100 mg daily for 12 weeks
Phototherapy and topical tacrolimus
mcq.e: Hypopigmented patches with **fine scale** on the **upper trunk** of a young adult in a hot, humid climate are **pityriasis versicolor**, caused by **Malassezia** yeast. Treat with **ketoconazole 2% shampoo** (or selenium sulphide) applied to the skin, or a topical azole, with an oral azole for extensive disease. Warn that **colour takes months to return** after cure and recurrence is common.
w: Wrong - steroids do not treat Malassezia and may worsen the infection.
Correct - ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied to the skin treats pityriasis versicolor.
Wrong - griseofulvin acts on dermatophytes and is ineffective against Malassezia.
Wrong - doxycycline is an antibiotic for acne, with no antifungal action.
Wrong - phototherapy and tacrolimus are used for vitiligo, which has no scale.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old woman with obesity and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes attends a Klinik Kesihatan with an itchy, sore rash under both breasts. There is a moist, bright, beefy-red plaque in the inframammary folds with a less defined edge and small satellite papules and pustules beyond the main plaque.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Tinea corporis
Inverse psoriasis
Erythrasma
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Cutaneous candidiasis
mcq.e: **Candidiasis** favours **moist skin folds** (inframammary, groin, axilla, abdominal folds) in people with **diabetes**, obesity or antibiotic use, and gives a **beefy-red** moist plaque with **satellite papules and pustules**. Tinea has a raised scaly edge with central clearing, and inverse psoriasis is well defined without satellites. Treat with a topical imidazole and keep the folds dry.
w: Wrong - tinea gives an annular plaque with a raised scaly edge and central clearing, not satellite pustules.
Wrong - inverse psoriasis is sharply defined and glazed, without satellite pustules.
Wrong - erythrasma is a brown, scaly, non-inflamed patch that fluoresces coral-red.
Wrong - seborrhoeic dermatitis has greasy yellowish scale and usually involves the scalp and face too.
Correct - a beefy-red fold rash with satellite pustules in a diabetic is cutaneous candidiasis.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old soldier who wears boots for long hours attends a Klinik Kesihatan with itchy, white, macerated skin and cracking between his 4th and 5th toes on both feet. You prescribe clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily. He asks how long he should use it.
What is the correct duration?
o: For 3 days only
Until the itch stops
For 6-12 weeks regardless of response
Until clear, then 2 more weeks
Twice weekly long-term
mcq.e: For tinea pedis, corporis and manuum, the slides recommend a topical imidazole or allylamine (e.g. **clotrimazole 1% 12-hourly**) **until clinical clearance plus an additional 2 weeks**. Stopping when the itch settles leaves viable fungus and causes relapse. Advise keeping the feet dry, changing socks and avoiding occlusive footwear.
w: Wrong - 3 days is far too short to eradicate a dermatophyte infection.
Wrong - itch settles before the fungus is cleared, so stopping then causes relapse.
Wrong - 6-12 weeks of oral griseofulvin is the tinea capitis regimen, not topical treatment for feet.
Correct - continue until clinical clearance and then for 2 more weeks.
Wrong - indefinite twice-weekly use is not the recommended treatment course.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old rubber tapper attends a Klinik Kesihatan with a dry, scaly rash on his right palm only for 6 months. The scaling is diffuse and fine, accentuated in the palmar creases. Both soles show similar dry scaling, and several toenails are thick and yellow. His left hand is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Irritant contact dermatitis of the hand
Palmoplantar plaque psoriasis
Dermatophyte infection of hand and feet
Dyshidrotic hand and foot eczema
Keratoderma of secondary syphilis
mcq.e: Diffuse dry palmar scaling that is **unilateral or asymmetric**, together with scaling of **both feet** and nail involvement, is the classic **two feet, one hand** pattern of **tinea manuum** arising from **tinea pedis** (the primary source). Confirm with KOH microscopy. Eczema and psoriasis are usually bilateral and symmetrical.
w: Wrong - irritant dermatitis would affect both hands with exposure and does not explain the foot and nail findings.
Wrong - psoriasis is usually bilateral and well demarcated, often with plaques elsewhere.
Correct - one hand plus both feet with nail disease is tinea manuum from tinea pedis.
Wrong - dyshidrotic eczema causes itchy deep-seated vesicles, usually symmetrical.
Wrong - syphilitic palmoplantar lesions are bilateral copper-coloured macules with other systemic features.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old mother is diagnosed with classical scabies at a Klinik Kesihatan and prescribed permethrin 5% cream. She has never used it before and asks exactly how to apply it.
Which instruction is correct?
o: Itchy areas only, every night for 3 nights
Neck down, wash off after 1 hour, single use
Face and scalp only, repeat after 1 month
Neck down overnight, repeat after 7 days
Whole body twice daily for 14 days
mcq.e: Apply **permethrin 5%** to cool, dry skin over the **whole body from the jawline or neck downwards** (including folds, genitals, between fingers and toes and under nails), leave on for **8-12 hours (overnight)**, then wash off. **Repeat after 7 days** to kill mites that hatch from surviving eggs. Reapply to any area washed during the treatment period, such as the hands.
w: Wrong - mites live in skin without symptoms, so treating only itchy areas leads to failure.
Wrong - a 1-hour contact time is too short and a single application misses newly hatched mites.
Wrong - adults with classical scabies are treated from the neck down, not just the face and scalp.
Correct - whole skin from neck down, left on overnight, repeated after 7 days.
Wrong - twice-daily use for 2 weeks is excessive and irritating without added benefit.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy is diagnosed with scabies at a Klinik Kesihatan. He lives with his parents, his 12-year-old sister and his grandmother. His mother is also itchy, but his father, sister and grandmother have no symptoms.
Which household members should be treated?
o: Only the itchy members now, others if symptoms
Only the index child, then review in 1 week
All household members at the same time today
Itchy members now, others one week later
Asymptomatic members with oral antihistamine
mcq.e: Itch in scabies is a **delayed hypersensitivity** reaction that can take **2-6 weeks** to appear, so contacts may be infested without symptoms. **All household and close contacts must be treated at the same time**, even if asymptomatic, otherwise mites pass back and forth (ping-pong re-infestation). Linen and clothing used in the previous few days should be decontaminated at the same time.
w: Wrong - waiting for symptoms allows asymptomatic carriers to re-infest the family.
Wrong - treating only the child leaves the infested mother and silent carriers untreated.
Correct - treat every household member simultaneously, regardless of symptoms.
Wrong - staggered treatment allows re-infestation between family members.
Wrong - antihistamines relieve itch but do not kill mites.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old woman returns to a Klinik Kesihatan 2 weeks after she and all her household contacts correctly used two applications of permethrin 5% one week apart. She is still itchy, especially at night. Examination shows a few excoriated papules but no new burrows or new vesicles.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Repeat permethrin course weekly for a month
Start oral ivermectin for treatment failure
Refer to dermatology for skin biopsy
Prescribe oral prednisolone for 2 weeks
Reassure, emollient and night antihistamine
mcq.e: **Post-scabetic itch** commonly persists for **2-4 weeks** after successful treatment because of the immune reaction to dead mites and their products. With correct treatment of all contacts and **no new burrows**, reassure and give **emollients, a sedating antihistamine at night and a mild topical steroid** if needed. Suspect failure only if new burrows or lesions appear after about 4 weeks.
w: Wrong - repeated scabicide irritates the skin and can worsen the itch.
Wrong - there is no evidence of treatment failure, as no new burrows are present.
Wrong - biopsy is unnecessary for expected post-scabetic itch.
Wrong - systemic steroids are not needed for post-scabetic itch.
Correct - post-scabetic itch: reassure, emollients and a night-time sedating antihistamine.

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old nursing home resident with advanced dementia is reviewed by the Klinik Kesihatan team. She has thick, grey, crusted, hyperkeratotic plaques on her hands, elbows and buttocks, with debris under her nails. She does not seem itchy. Three care staff have recently developed itchy rashes.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral ivermectin plus permethrin, with isolation
Single application of permethrin 5% cream only
Potent topical steroid under occlusion to plaques
Oral terbinafine for 6 weeks with nail clipping
Keratolytic emollient alone and review in 1 month
mcq.e: Thick crusts with minimal itch in a **neurologically impaired or immunocompromised** patient, with spread to carers, is **crusted (Norwegian) scabies**. It carries a **huge mite burden** and is **extremely contagious**. Management is **oral ivermectin plus topical permethrin**, keratolytics, nail care, **isolation with contact precautions**, and treatment of all staff and resident contacts.
w: Correct - crusted scabies needs oral ivermectin with topical scabicide, isolation and contact treatment.
Wrong - a single topical application cannot penetrate thick crusts or clear a huge mite load.
Wrong - steroids would further suppress immunity and increase mite numbers.
Wrong - terbinafine treats dermatophytes, not mites.
Wrong - keratolytics are an adjunct only; this extremely contagious infestation must be treated now.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of scalp itching and poor sleep. Her teacher has noticed her scratching. Examination shows small white oval specks firmly attached to hair shafts close to the scalp behind the ears, and a few scratch marks on the neck.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral ivermectin single dose for the whole class
Permethrin 1% lotion, repeat in 7-10 days
Permethrin 5% cream from the neck down
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly
Shave the head with no medication needed
mcq.e: Nits firmly attached near the scalp with itch indicate **head lice** (Pediculus humanus capitis). Treat with **permethrin 1% lotion** (or malathion), **repeated after 7-10 days** to kill newly hatched lice, plus **wet combing with a fine-toothed nit comb**. Check and treat affected family members. Permethrin 5% cream from the neck down is the scabies regimen.
w: Wrong - oral ivermectin is not first-line for head lice and mass treatment of a class is not indicated.
Correct - head lice: permethrin 1% lotion, repeated in 7-10 days, with nit combing.
Wrong - this is the scabies regimen and spares the scalp, where head lice live.
Wrong - ketoconazole shampoo treats fungal and seborrhoeic conditions, not lice.
Wrong - shaving is distressing and unnecessary; effective treatments are available.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with known atopic eczema is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with a 2-day history of a rapidly worsening, painful rash on her face and neck. She is febrile (38.6 °C) and miserable. Examination shows clusters of monomorphic, punched-out erosions with haemorrhagic crusts over her existing eczema.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start oral cloxacillin and review in 48 hours in clinic
Step up to a potent topical steroid with wet wrap therapy
Refer urgently the same day for systemic aciclovir treatment
Take a skin swab and review once the culture report returns
Apply topical mupirocin and continue the usual emollient
mcq.e: Monomorphic **punched-out erosions** with fever on a background of atopic eczema is **eczema herpeticum** (disseminated HSV). The Malaysian AE CPG lists it as an **urgent referral**: it needs systemic aciclovir without delay and eye review if periocular. The trap is to treat it as a bacterial flare or to escalate topical steroids, which spreads the virus.
w: Wrong - an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic alone misses the herpes virus, and a 48-hour delay risks dissemination.
Wrong - potent steroids and wet wraps suppress local immunity and can worsen a herpetic infection.
Correct - suspected eczema herpeticum is an urgent referral for systemic antiviral therapy.
Wrong - waiting for culture delays antiviral treatment; the clinical picture is enough to act.
Wrong - topical antibiotics treat impetiginised eczema, not a disseminated viral infection.

mcq.stem:
A 7-month-old boy has had itchy, red, scaly patches on both cheeks and on the extensor surfaces of his forearms for 6 weeks. His mother applies emollients several times a day. There are no erosions, crusts or other signs of infection.
Which topical corticosteroid is most appropriate for the facial lesions?
o: Hydrocortisone 1% cream once or twice daily for a short course
Betamethasone valerate 0.1% cream twice daily for two weeks
Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once daily for one week
Mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment twice daily until clear
Fluticasone propionate 0.05% cream twice daily for one month
mcq.e: Topical steroid potency is chosen by **severity AND site**. Facial skin, especially in infants, is thin and absorbs well, so a **mild-potency** steroid such as hydrocortisone 1% is used for short courses alongside emollients. Potent and very potent steroids on the face risk atrophy, telangiectasia and perioral dermatitis.
w: Correct - mild-potency hydrocortisone is the appropriate choice for an infant's face.
Wrong - betamethasone valerate 0.1% is potent and should not be used on an infant's face.
Wrong - clobetasol is very potent and is avoided on the face, particularly in infants.
Wrong - mometasone is potent; continuing 'until clear' on the face invites atrophy.
Wrong - fluticasone is a potent steroid; a month of twice-daily use on an infant's face is excessive.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy with moderate atopic eczema has had 5 flares in the last 6 months, always at the same flexural sites on the elbows and knees. Each flare clears within a week of a moderate-potency topical steroid but recurs within weeks of stopping. He uses emollients daily.
What is the best next step to prevent further flares?
o: Continuous daily moderate-potency steroid to the flexures for three months
Prophylactic oral antihistamine at night throughout the school term
A 3-month course of oral prednisolone tapered over the final month
Stop topical steroids entirely and use emollients alone between flares
Fluticasone 0.05% cream once or twice weekly to the usual flare sites
mcq.e: Frequent flares at the same sites call for **proactive (weekend) therapy**: after clearing, apply fluticasone propionate 0.05% cream **1-2 times a week** to previously affected skin, plus daily emollients. This keeps subclinical inflammation suppressed with far less steroid exposure than continuous use. Systemic steroids are not used for maintenance in eczema.
w: Wrong - continuous daily steroid for months increases the risk of atrophy without added benefit over proactive use.
Wrong - oral antihistamines do not prevent eczema flares; sedating ones only help sleep.
Wrong - systemic steroids cause rebound flares and serious side effects and are not maintenance therapy.
Wrong - this is what he is already doing, and it is failing.
Correct - intermittent proactive fluticasone to usual flare sites reduces relapses.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old woman has recurrent eczema on her eyelids and around her eyes. Hydrocortisone 1% cream helps, but the rash returns whenever she stops, and she has used it on and off for most of the past year. She is worried about skin thinning.
Which treatment is most appropriate for long-term control of this site?
o: Betamethasone valerate 0.1% cream daily as maintenance
Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment as a steroid-sparing agent
Clobetasol 0.05% cream for flares, then emollient only
Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily, tapered over two weeks
Mupirocin 2% ointment twice daily with an emollient
mcq.e: **Topical calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus 0.1% ointment in adults, pimecrolimus 1% cream) do not cause skin atrophy, so they suit thin-skinned sites such as the **eyelids, face and flexures** when steroids are needed long term. Warn about transient burning on application. Escalating steroid potency on the eyelids risks atrophy, glaucoma and cataract.
w: Wrong - a potent steroid used daily on the eyelids risks atrophy, glaucoma and cataract.
Correct - a calcineurin inhibitor controls eyelid eczema without causing skin thinning.
Wrong - very potent steroids must not be used on the eyelids.
Wrong - systemic steroids are not used for localised eczema and cause rebound flares.
Wrong - there is no infection; a topical antibiotic does not treat the inflammation.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl with atopic eczema attends a Klinik Kesihatan for review. The medical officer wants a single severity score that combines the extent of involvement, the intensity of signs such as erythema and lichenification, AND the child's subjective itch and sleep loss, to track response to treatment.
Which tool is most appropriate?
o: Eczema Area and Severity Index
Children's Dermatology Life Quality Index
Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure
SCORing Atopic Dermatitis index
Investigator's Global Assessment
mcq.e: **SCORAD** is the only listed tool that combines **extent** (rule of nines), **intensity** of six signs and **subjective symptoms** (itch and sleep loss). EASI scores extent and signs only, IGA is a single global grade, POEM is patient-reported symptoms only, and CDLQI measures quality of life rather than severity.
w: Wrong - EASI scores extent and intensity of signs but has no itch or sleep component.
Wrong - CDLQI measures quality of life, not disease severity.
Wrong - POEM is purely patient-reported symptoms, with no clinician-scored signs or extent.
Correct - SCORAD combines extent, intensity of signs and subjective itch and sleep loss.
Wrong - IGA is a single overall clinician grade without symptom scoring.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has a 4-month history of an itchy rash that comes and goes. His father has allergic rhinitis. Examination shows generally dry skin with ill-defined, excoriated, thickened plaques with exaggerated skin markings in the antecubital and popliteal fossae and around the neck. The finger webs, palms and genitalia are spared, and no burrows are seen.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Flexural (inverse) psoriasis
Classical scabies infestation
Tinea corporis (ringworm)
Atopic eczema (dermatitis)
Allergic contact dermatitis
mcq.e: Chronic relapsing itch, **xerosis**, **lichenification** in the **flexures** and a family history of atopy fit atopic eczema (UK Working Party criteria). Scabies favours finger webs, wrists and genitalia with burrows; inverse psoriasis gives sharp, shiny, non-scaly plaques that are less itchy; tinea forms annular plaques with an active edge.
w: Wrong - inverse psoriasis gives well-demarcated, shiny plaques in body folds, not ill-defined lichenified eczema with xerosis.
Wrong - scabies involves finger webs, wrists and genitalia with burrows, which are absent.
Wrong - tinea causes annular plaques with a scaly active edge and central clearing.
Correct - flexural lichenified itchy plaques, dry skin and family atopy indicate atopic eczema.
Wrong - contact dermatitis is confined to the site of contact with an allergen, not symmetrical flexures.

mcq.stem:
A 6-week-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan because of a scaly rash on the scalp. He feeds well and does not seem itchy or irritable. Examination shows thick, greasy, yellowish scales and crusts on the vertex of the scalp, with salmon-pink patches behind the ears and in the nappy area, including the skin creases.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Infantile atopic eczema
Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis
Tinea capitis with kerion
Scabies in a young infant
Irritant napkin (diaper) dermatitis
mcq.e: Onset in the **first weeks of life**, **greasy yellow scales** on the scalp (cradle cap), involvement of the **flexures and creases** and a **non-itchy**, contented baby point to infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis. Infantile atopic eczema usually starts after 2-3 months, is itchy and favours the cheeks and extensors. Irritant napkin dermatitis spares the skin creases.
w: Wrong - atopic eczema is itchy, usually starts after 2-3 months and favours cheeks and extensors.
Correct - greasy yellow scalp scale and flexural involvement in a non-itchy young infant is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Wrong - tinea capitis is rare in young infants and a kerion is a boggy, pustular swelling.
Wrong - infant scabies is intensely itchy with papules and vesicles on palms, soles and trunk.
Wrong - irritant napkin dermatitis spares the creases and does not explain the scalp scale.

mcq.stem:
A 3-month-old girl has had thick, adherent yellow scales on her scalp for 3 weeks. She is thriving, is not itchy and has no rash elsewhere. Her mother is anxious and asks what she should do.
What is the most appropriate first-line advice?
o: Soften scales with vegetable oil, mild baby shampoo and gentle brushing
Apply betamethasone valerate 0.1% scalp application twice daily for two weeks
Start oral griseofulvin for six weeks after sending scalp scrapings
Pick off the crusts daily with a fine comb after a hot bath
Refer to dermatology for patch testing to identify the allergen
mcq.e: Cradle cap is benign and self-limiting. First-line care is **scalp hygiene**: soften scales with **vegetable oil**, wash regularly with **mild baby shampoo** and **gently brush** scales off. Ketoconazole 2% cream or mild hydrocortisone are added only if it is persistent or inflamed; potent steroids and oral antifungals are not needed.
w: Correct - oil to soften, mild shampoo and gentle brushing are the first-line measures for cradle cap.
Wrong - a potent steroid is unnecessary for a non-inflamed, self-limiting infant scalp condition.
Wrong - this is not tinea capitis; oral griseofulvin is not indicated.
Wrong - forcibly picking crusts and hot water traumatise the scalp and risk infection.
Wrong - cradle cap is not an allergic contact dermatitis; patch testing has no role.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man has a 1-year history of itchy scalp flaking with red, greasy, scaly patches in his eyebrows and nasolabial folds. It worsens when he is stressed. His nails are normal and there are no plaques on his elbows or knees.
What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for six weeks with a tar shampoo
Clobetasol 0.05% scalp lotion and cream to the face twice daily
Oral doxycycline 100 mg daily for three months with a face wash
Topical calcipotriol to the scalp and to the facial patches daily
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly plus 2% cream BD to the face
mcq.e: Greasy scale on the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds is adult **seborrhoeic dermatitis**, driven by **Malassezia** overgrowth. Treatment targets the yeast: **ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly** and ketoconazole 2% cream BD to the face, with short courses of hydrocortisone 1% for flares. Potent steroids on the face are avoided.
w: Wrong - oral terbinafine treats dermatophytes, not Malassezia-driven seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Wrong - a very potent steroid on the face risks atrophy and rebound; only mild steroids are used briefly.
Wrong - oral doxycycline treats acne and rosacea, not seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Wrong - calcipotriol is a psoriasis treatment and irritates facial skin.
Correct - topical ketoconazole reduces Malassezia colonisation on the scalp and face.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman has a recurrent itchy, eczematous rash on both earlobes and a well-defined patch just below her umbilicus. It began after she started wearing costume jewellery and flares within 1-2 days of re-exposure. Her hands are unaffected.
Which investigation will best confirm the cause?
o: Skin scrapings for KOH microscopy
Serum total and specific IgE levels
Patch testing with a baseline series
Skin prick testing to common allergens
Punch biopsy for routine histology
mcq.e: Eczema at sites of metal contact (earrings, jeans stud) with a **delayed** flare after re-exposure suggests **allergic contact dermatitis to nickel**, a type IV (cell-mediated) reaction. The gold-standard test is **patch testing**. Skin prick tests and IgE detect immediate type I allergy and are the wrong mechanism.
w: Wrong - KOH microscopy looks for fungal elements, which do not explain a jewellery-related rash.
Wrong - IgE levels reflect type I allergy; contact dermatitis is a type IV reaction.
Correct - patch testing identifies the contact allergen in delayed hypersensitivity.
Wrong - prick testing detects immediate IgE-mediated allergy, not contact allergy.
Wrong - histology shows non-specific eczema and cannot identify the allergen.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of rapidly spreading red, greasy scaling over his scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, central chest and groin that has not responded to ketoconazole shampoo and cream. He had shingles last year and now has white plaques on his tongue that scrape off.
Which investigation is most important to request next?
o: Patch testing with a baseline series
Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c
Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence
HIV serology after pre-test counselling
Thyroid function tests and anti-TPO
mcq.e: Seborrhoeic dermatitis that is **sudden, severe, extensive or treatment-resistant** in a young adult is a recognised marker of **HIV infection**, especially with other clues such as shingles in a young person and oral candidiasis. HIV testing with counselling is the key next step. Parkinson disease is the other classic association in older adults.
w: Wrong - patch testing is for allergic contact dermatitis, which does not fit this distribution.
Wrong - diabetes can predispose to candidiasis but does not explain severe seborrhoeic dermatitis with early shingles.
Wrong - immunofluorescence is used for lupus or bullous disease, not seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Correct - severe, resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis with oral thrush and shingles in a young adult warrants HIV testing.
Wrong - thyroid disease does not explain this cluster of opportunistic features.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends with her mother about 'pimples' on her forehead and nose for 6 months. Examination shows numerous open and closed comedones with a few small papules, and no nodules or scarring. She is not distressed and wants a simple regimen.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Topical adapalene gel applied thinly at night to the whole area
Oral doxycycline 100 mg daily for three months as monotherapy
Topical clindamycin gel twice daily used on its own long term
Oral isotretinoin 0.5 mg/kg daily started at the Klinik Kesihatan
Combined oral contraceptive pill as the sole initial treatment
mcq.e: Mild, mainly **comedonal** acne is treated topically. **Topical retinoids** (e.g. adapalene) normalise follicular keratinisation and are the key anti-comedonal agent, applied thinly to the whole area, not just spots. Antibiotics, topical or oral, are never used alone because of resistance, and isotretinoin is specialist-only for severe acne.
w: Correct - a topical retinoid applied to the whole affected area is first line for comedonal acne.
Wrong - oral antibiotics are for moderate to severe inflammatory acne and are never used as monotherapy.
Wrong - topical antibiotics alone breed C. acnes resistance and do little for comedones.
Wrong - isotretinoin is reserved for severe or refractory acne and is started by a dermatologist.
Wrong - hormonal therapy is an option for selected women, not first-line sole therapy for mild comedonal acne.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old man has had acne on his face, chest and back for 2 years. Examination shows many inflamed papules and pustules over the face and upper back, with comedones but no nodules or scarring. Twelve weeks of topical benzoyl peroxide with adapalene, used correctly, has helped only slightly.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Add topical clindamycin and stop the benzoyl peroxide gel
Switch to oral doxycycline alone and stop all topical agents
Add oral doxycycline while continuing the topical combination
Refer urgently to dermatology to start oral isotretinoin now
Add oral prednisolone for two weeks to settle the inflammation
mcq.e: Moderate inflammatory acne involving the trunk that fails topical therapy warrants an **oral antibiotic (doxycycline)** combined with **topical benzoyl peroxide and/or a retinoid**. Benzoyl peroxide reduces antibiotic resistance and the retinoid treats comedones. Review at about 3 months; isotretinoin is for severe or refractory disease.
w: Wrong - stopping benzoyl peroxide removes the agent that prevents antibiotic resistance.
Wrong - antibiotics must never be used alone; topical therapy continues alongside.
Correct - an oral antibiotic plus continued topical benzoyl peroxide and retinoid is the right step-up.
Wrong - there are no nodules or scarring, and an adequate oral antibiotic trial has not yet been given.
Wrong - systemic steroids are not a treatment for acne vulgaris and can cause steroid acne.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old woman has multiple painful inflammatory nodules and cysts on her face and back with early atrophic scarring (CASS grade 5). She is upset about her appearance but denies low mood or self-harm thoughts, and she is systemically well with no fever or joint pain.
What is the most appropriate referral plan?
o: Same-day emergency referral to the hospital dermatology team
No referral; treat with topical retinoid and review in 6 months
Routine referral after a further 6 months of oral antibiotics
Same-day psychiatric referral for assessment of suicide risk
Dermatology referral to be seen early, within about 2 weeks
mcq.e: The Malaysian acne CPG separates urgency: **acne fulminans** or **major depression/suicidal behaviour** need **urgent** referral, whereas **severe nodulocystic acne (CASS 4-5)** or severe psychosocial distress should be **seen early, within 2 weeks**, because scarring is permanent and isotretinoin is specialist-initiated. She has no systemic or psychiatric red flags.
w: Wrong - same-day referral is for acne fulminans; she is systemically well.
Wrong - nodulocystic acne with scarring needs specialist care, not topical therapy alone.
Wrong - delaying for months risks further permanent scarring.
Wrong - she has no low mood or suicidal thoughts, though mood should be monitored.
Correct - CASS 4-5 nodulocystic acne should be seen by dermatology within about 2 weeks.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy with moderate acne suddenly develops painful, ulcerated, haemorrhagic nodules with crusts on his chest and back over 10 days. His temperature is 38.4 °C and he has painful knees and malaise. He has not started any new medication.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start oral doxycycline and review at the clinic in 4 weeks
Refer urgently to dermatology on the same day for assessment
Dermatology referral to be seen routinely within 3 months
Swab the lesions and start topical clindamycin in the meantime
Prescribe paracetamol and review in 2 weeks if not settling
mcq.e: Sudden ulcerating, haemorrhagic nodular acne with **fever, arthralgia and malaise** is **acne fulminans**, an **urgent referral** in the Malaysian CPG. It needs specialist systemic treatment (typically oral steroids before or with low-dose isotretinoin). Ordinary antibiotics or delayed review are inadequate.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics do not control acne fulminans and a 4-week delay is unsafe.
Correct - systemic features with ulcerating nodules suggest acne fulminans, which needs urgent referral.
Wrong - routine referral is far too slow for a systemic inflammatory acne variant.
Wrong - this is not a simple infection; topical antibiotics will not help.
Wrong - symptomatic treatment alone misses an urgent condition.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman has persistent acne along her jawline despite 3 months of appropriate topical therapy. Her menstrual cycles occur every 45-60 days, she has coarse hair on her chin and lower abdomen, and her BMI is 31 kg/m².
Which investigation is most appropriate to request?
o: Pus swab from a pustule for culture and sensitivity
Serum IgE and skin prick tests to food allergens
Skin biopsy of an inflamed papule for histology
Serum testosterone, LH/FSH and a pelvic ultrasound
Skin scrapings for KOH microscopy of the jawline
mcq.e: Acne is diagnosed clinically, but the CPG advises **endocrine tests** when **hyperandrogenism** is suspected. Oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, obesity and treatment-resistant jawline acne suggest **polycystic ovary syndrome**. Finding it changes management (e.g. hormonal therapy, weight and metabolic care).
w: Wrong - microbiology is for suspected staphylococcal or Gram-negative folliculitis, not suspected PCOS.
Wrong - food allergy testing has no role in acne assessment.
Wrong - biopsy is not needed for typical acne.
Correct - features of hyperandrogenism call for hormonal tests and ovarian imaging for PCOS.
Wrong - fungal scrapings do not address the endocrine clues.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant has mild to moderate papulopustular acne on her face. She asks for a cream to treat it.
Which topical agent is most appropriate?
o: Tretinoin 0.025% cream at night
Adapalene 0.1% gel at night
Tazarotene 0.1% cream at night
Clindamycin 1% gel alone twice daily
Azelaic acid 20% cream twice daily
mcq.e: **Retinoids** (topical tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene and oral isotretinoin) are **avoided in pregnancy** because of teratogenic risk. **Azelaic acid** (and benzoyl peroxide) are considered safe and treat both comedones and inflammation. Topical antibiotics should never be used alone.
w: Wrong - topical retinoids such as tretinoin are avoided in pregnancy.
Wrong - adapalene is a retinoid and should not be used in pregnancy.
Wrong - tazarotene is a retinoid that is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - antibiotic monotherapy promotes resistance; it must be paired with benzoyl peroxide.
Correct - azelaic acid is effective and considered safe in pregnancy.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old girl presents with a sudden eruption of many small (3-8 mm) scaly pink papules scattered over her trunk and proximal limbs. Two weeks earlier she had a sore throat with fever. No single larger patch preceded the rash, and the scale is silvery rather than a fine collarette.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Pityriasis rosea
Secondary syphilis
Guttate psoriasis
Pityriasis versicolor
Tinea corporis
mcq.e: Guttate ('drop-like') psoriasis is a **sudden shower of small scaly papules** on the trunk and limbs, classically **1-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection**, in children and young adults. Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch and has collarette scale in a 'Christmas tree' pattern. Guttate psoriasis can resolve or evolve into chronic plaque disease.
w: Wrong - pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch and shows a fine collarette of scale.
Wrong - secondary syphilis often involves palms and soles and is unlikely after a sore throat in a 14-year-old.
Correct - small silvery-scaled drop-like papules after a streptococcal sore throat suggest guttate psoriasis.
Wrong - pityriasis versicolor gives hypo- or hyperpigmented macules with fine scale, not an acute post-infective eruption.
Wrong - tinea causes a few annular plaques with an active edge, not a sudden widespread shower.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man has chronic plaque psoriasis that was well controlled with topical therapy. Over the past 6 weeks he has developed a marked flare with many new plaques. Two months ago, after a myocardial infarction, he was started on several new medicines. He denies recent infection, alcohol excess or stress.
Which drug is the most likely trigger?
o: Propranolol
Amlodipine
Metformin
Atorvastatin
Omeprazole
mcq.e: **Beta-blockers** are classic triggers of psoriasis flares, along with **lithium**, **antimalarials** (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine), **NSAIDs** and the **withdrawal of systemic steroids**. When a stable patient flares, always review recent medicines; discuss alternatives with the prescribing team rather than stopping cardioprotective drugs abruptly.
w: Correct - beta-blockers such as propranolol are well-known to provoke psoriasis flares.
Wrong - amlodipine is not a recognised trigger of psoriasis.
Wrong - metformin does not worsen psoriasis.
Wrong - statins are not a classic psoriasis trigger.
Wrong - proton pump inhibitors are not associated with psoriasis flares.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman with extensive plaque psoriasis was given a 2-week course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily by a private clinic. Five days after finishing it she presents unwell, with fever of 38.9 °C and widespread painful, red skin studded with sheets of tiny sterile pustules.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Erythrodermic psoriasis
Generalised pustular psoriasis
Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis
Disseminated bacterial folliculitis
