Eczema herpeticum
mcq.e: **Withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids** is a classic trigger of **generalised pustular (von Zumbusch) psoriasis**: fever, malaise and sheets of sterile pustules on red skin. This is why systemic steroids are avoided in psoriasis. Generalised pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis are **urgent referrals** because of fluid, temperature and infection risks.
w: Wrong - erythrodermic psoriasis is widespread redness and scaling without sheets of pustules.
Correct - sterile pustules on red skin with fever after steroid withdrawal is generalised pustular psoriasis.
Wrong - AGEP is a drug reaction usually days after starting a new drug (often antibiotics), not after steroid withdrawal in known psoriasis.
Wrong - folliculitis gives follicle-centred pustules, not sheets of sterile pustules with systemic illness.
Wrong - eczema herpeticum shows punched-out erosions on eczematous skin, not sterile pustules.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man presents for the first time with chronic plaque psoriasis on his trunk and limbs. He has had no treatment so far. The plaques together cover an area equal to about 14 of his own palms (hand including the fingers). His DLQI score is 8. He has no joint symptoms.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Classify as mild because DLQI is 10 or less; topical therapy only
Start oral prednisolone to bring the extensive plaques under control
Start topical therapy and refer only if no response after 12 weeks
Start topical therapy and refer to dermatology as BSA exceeds 10%
Apply coal tar to all plaques including the face and body folds
mcq.e: One patient palm including fingers is about **1% BSA**, so 14 palms is about **14% BSA**. Psoriasis is **mild only if BSA ≤10% AND DLQI ≤10**; BSA above 10% makes it **moderate to severe**, which the Malaysian CPG lists as a reason to refer to dermatology (for phototherapy or systemic therapy), while starting topical treatment meanwhile. The 12-week rule applies to mild disease that fails topical therapy.
w: Wrong - severity needs both measures; BSA above 10% alone makes it moderate to severe.
Wrong - systemic steroids are avoided in psoriasis because withdrawal can trigger pustular or erythrodermic flares.
Wrong - the 12-week trial is for mild disease; extensive disease qualifies for referral now.
Correct - about 14% BSA is moderate to severe psoriasis and should be referred while topical treatment starts.
Wrong - tar is not used on the face, genitalia or body folds and is impractical over extensive areas.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has plaque psoriasis on her elbows, knees and lower back. The total affected area is estimated at 6% of her body surface area. You prescribe a topical corticosteroid ointment and explain the fingertip unit (FTU).
How much ointment should she apply to cover all the plaques at each application?
o: 3 FTU, about 1.5 g
6 FTU, about 3 g
3 FTU, about 3 g
12 FTU, about 6 g
1 FTU, about 0.5 g
mcq.e: One **fingertip unit** (ointment squeezed from the tip to the first crease of an adult index finger) weighs about **0.5 g** and covers about **2% BSA** (two adult palms). For 6% BSA she needs 6 ÷ 2 = **3 FTU = about 1.5 g** per application. Using FTUs avoids both under-treatment and steroid overuse.
w: Correct - 6% BSA needs 3 FTU, and 3 x 0.5 g is about 1.5 g.
Wrong - this assumes 1 FTU covers only 1% BSA; it covers about 2%.
Wrong - the FTU count is right but each FTU is about 0.5 g, not 1 g.
Wrong - this is four times the required amount and wastes steroid.
Wrong - 1 FTU covers only about 2% BSA, a third of her plaques.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old obese man has sharply demarcated, shiny, red plaques with little scale in both groins and in the natal cleft. Skin scrapings are negative for fungal elements. He also has typical thick scaly plaques on both elbows.
Which topical treatment is most appropriate for the groin and natal cleft?
o: Coal tar 5% ointment applied at night to the folds
Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice daily
Salicylic acid 6% ointment to lift the scale first
Dithranol 0.5% short-contact cream once daily
Hydrocortisone 1% cream short course to the folds
mcq.e: This is **inverse (flexural) psoriasis**. Skin in the folds is thin and occluded, so it absorbs steroid readily: use a **low-potency steroid** in a **cream** base for short courses (calcineurin inhibitors are an alternative). The CPG advises **tar not on the face, genitalia or body folds**, and dithranol and salicylic acid are too irritant there.
w: Wrong - tar is irritant and staining and is not used in body folds or genitalia.
Wrong - a very potent steroid under occlusion in the folds causes atrophy and striae.
Wrong - inverse psoriasis has little scale and salicylic acid irritates flexural skin.
Wrong - dithranol burns and stains and is unsuitable for flexures and genital skin.
Correct - a mild steroid cream used briefly suits thin, occluded flexural skin.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman with scalp and nail psoriasis reports 3 months of pain and swelling of the whole right second toe and of the distal interphalangeal joints of two fingers, with morning stiffness lasting about 1 hour. Her nails show pitting and onycholysis.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure; joint symptoms are common with nail psoriasis
Prescribe allopurinol after checking the serum uric acid
Refer to rheumatology to assess for psoriatic arthritis
Start a short course of oral prednisolone for the joints
Increase the potency of topical steroid on the nails
mcq.e: **Dactylitis**, **DIP joint** involvement, inflammatory morning stiffness and **nail disease** strongly suggest **psoriatic arthritis**. The Malaysian psoriasis CPG advises **rheumatology referral** for suspected PsA, because early disease-modifying treatment prevents joint destruction. Nail psoriasis is a marker of higher PsA risk, not a reason to dismiss joint pain.
w: Wrong - inflammatory joint symptoms are a warning sign, and delay risks erosive joint damage.
Wrong - gout is acute and episodic; dactylitis with DIP disease and nail pitting points to psoriatic arthritis.
Correct - suspected psoriatic arthritis should be referred to rheumatology for assessment and DMARD planning.
Wrong - systemic steroids mask symptoms and can trigger a severe psoriasis flare on withdrawal.
Wrong - topical steroids on the nails do not treat inflammatory arthritis.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of a red, slightly swollen rash across both cheeks and the bridge of her nose that appeared after a beach holiday. The nasolabial folds are spared. There are no pustules, comedones or greasy scale. She also reports painful wrists and painless mouth ulcers.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Facial rosacea
Acute cutaneous lupus
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Contact dermatitis to sunscreen
Sunburn (acute UV injury)
mcq.e: A photosensitive **malar ('butterfly') rash** that **spares the nasolabial folds** and lasts hours to days is **localised acute cutaneous lupus**, which is commonly associated with **systemic lupus** (here, arthralgia and painless oral ulcers). Seborrhoeic dermatitis typically involves the nasolabial folds with greasy scale; rosacea has papules, pustules and flushing.
w: Wrong - rosacea has flushing, telangiectasia and papulopustules, and lacks joint pain or oral ulcers.
Correct - a photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds with arthralgia and oral ulcers is acute cutaneous lupus.
Wrong - seborrhoeic dermatitis characteristically involves the nasolabial folds with greasy scale.
Wrong - contact dermatitis follows the area of application and would not explain arthralgia or mouth ulcers.
Wrong - sunburn affects all exposed skin, including the folds, and has no systemic features.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman has a 2-month history of red, annular and polycyclic scaly plaques with central clearing on her upper back, the V of her neck and her outer arms. They flare after sun exposure. Her face is largely spared, and KOH microscopy of the scale is negative.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subacute cutaneous lupus
Tinea corporis (ringworm)
Discoid lupus erythematosus
Granuloma annulare
Chronic plaque psoriasis
mcq.e: **Subacute cutaneous lupus** gives **annular, polycyclic or psoriasiform** plaques on **sun-exposed trunk and upper limbs**, healing with dyspigmentation but **no scarring**. It is linked to anti-Ro antibodies and can be drug-induced (e.g. thiazides, PPIs, terbinafine). Negative KOH helps exclude tinea, its main look-alike.
w: Correct - photosensitive annular polycyclic plaques on the upper trunk and arms suggest subacute cutaneous lupus.
Wrong - tinea is excluded by negative KOH and is not photo-distributed.
Wrong - discoid lupus favours the scalp, ears and face and leaves scarring.
Wrong - granuloma annulare has smooth, non-scaly papules in rings, usually on hands and feet.
Wrong - plaque psoriasis favours extensor surfaces and is not annular with central clearing after sun.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old woman has a 6-month history of well-defined, red, scaly plaques on her scalp and ears. Lifting the scale shows spiky plugs on its underside, and the older scalp lesions have left smooth, shiny patches with no hair regrowth. She is otherwise well.
Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
o: Wood's lamp examination of the affected scalp
Fungal culture of plucked hairs from the patch
Serum anti-dsDNA antibody titre
Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence
Dermoscopy-guided scalp scraping for KOH
mcq.e: Scaly plaques with **follicular plugging** (the 'carpet tack' sign) on the scalp and ears that heal with **scarring alopecia** are **discoid lupus**. Cutaneous lupus is confirmed by **skin biopsy for histopathology and direct immunofluorescence**; blood tests and ANA/ENA screen for systemic disease but cannot confirm the skin diagnosis. Early treatment limits permanent hair loss.
w: Wrong - Wood's lamp detects some fungal scalp infections; it cannot confirm lupus.
Wrong - scarring alopecia with follicular plugging is not tinea capitis.
Wrong - anti-dsDNA is often negative in isolated discoid lupus and does not confirm the skin lesion.
Correct - biopsy with histology and immunofluorescence confirms cutaneous lupus.
Wrong - KOH looks for fungus, which this scarring picture does not suggest.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman with biopsy-proven cutaneous lupus and no systemic involvement on blood tests asks how she can reduce flares. She works outdoors as a traffic warden and smokes 10 cigarettes a day.
Which advice is most important?
o: Gradual sunbed exposure to build up her tolerance to UV light
SPF 15 sunscreen applied once in the morning before work
Strict dairy-free, gluten-free diet to dampen autoimmunity
Cut down to 5 cigarettes daily, as smoking does not affect lupus
SPF 50+ sunscreen, sun-protective clothing and quit smoking
mcq.e: UV light triggers cutaneous lupus, so **strict photoprotection** is the foundation: broad-spectrum **SPF 50+** sunscreen reapplied through the day, hats and protective clothing. **Smoking worsens CLE** and reduces the effect of antimalarials, so complete **cessation** (e.g. via mQuit services) is advised. Vitamin D supplementation is recommended because of sun avoidance.
w: Wrong - any extra UV exposure provokes flares; there is no 'tolerance' approach in lupus.
Wrong - SPF 15 once a day is inadequate for an outdoor worker; SPF 50+ reapplied is needed.
Wrong - restrictive diets have no proven role in cutaneous lupus.
Wrong - smoking worsens cutaneous lupus and blunts antimalarial response; she should stop completely.
Correct - high-SPF sunscreen, protective clothing and smoking cessation are the key self-care measures.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old boy with obesity (BMI 34 kg/m²) has dark, velvety, thickened skin on the back of his neck and in both axillae. His mother thinks it is dirt that will not wash off. His fasting plasma glucose is 6.4 mmol/L.
Which mechanism best explains the skin change?
o: Melanocyte stimulation by excess ACTH from the pituitary
Cholesterol deposition in dermal macrophages from dyslipidaemia
Hyperinsulinaemia activating IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes
Glycosaminoglycan deposition driven by TSH-receptor antibodies
Microangiopathy with haemosiderin deposits after minor trauma
mcq.e: **Acanthosis nigricans** is a marker of **insulin resistance**. High insulin levels activate **IGF-1 receptors** on keratinocytes and fibroblasts, driving proliferation, epidermal thickening and hyperpigmentation in flexures. Treat the cause: weight loss, activity and glycaemic control, and screen for diabetes (his fasting glucose is in the impaired range).
w: Wrong - ACTH excess causes diffuse pigmentation (e.g. Addison disease), not velvety flexural thickening.
Wrong - cholesterol deposition produces xanthelasma or xanthomas, not velvety plaques.
Correct - hyperinsulinaemia stimulates IGF-1 receptors, causing thickened, pigmented flexural skin.
Wrong - this is the mechanism of pretibial myxoedema in Graves disease.
Wrong - this describes diabetic dermopathy (shin spots), not acanthosis nigricans.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old thin man presents with 2 months of rapidly spreading, itchy, dark, velvety thickening of his axillae, palms and the skin around his mouth. He has lost 8 kg and has early satiety. He does not have diabetes; his fasting glucose and HbA1c are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure, and advise weight reduction and a low-sugar diet
Urgent referral to evaluate for an internal malignancy
Start metformin for presumed insulin resistance
Topical retinoid and review the skin in 3 months
Check thyroid function and repeat HbA1c in a year
mcq.e: Acanthosis nigricans that is **sudden, extensive, itchy**, involves the **palms or mucosa** and occurs in an **older, non-obese** person without insulin resistance suggests **malignant acanthosis nigricans**, most often from a **gastric adenocarcinoma**. With weight loss and early satiety he needs urgent referral for endoscopy and cancer work-up.
w: Wrong - he is thin with normal glucose; reassurance misses a paraneoplastic sign.
Correct - sudden extensive acanthosis nigricans with weight loss needs urgent malignancy work-up.
Wrong - there is no evidence of insulin resistance to treat.
Wrong - treating the skin delays diagnosis of the likely underlying cancer.
Wrong - a year's delay is unsafe given the red flags.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years, followed up for retinopathy and nephropathy, notices several small, round, brown, slightly depressed, finely scaly patches on both shins. They are asymptomatic and some older ones have faded. There is no ulceration, induration or yellow discolouration.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Necrobiosis lipoidica
Pretibial myxoedema
Stasis (venous) dermatitis
Lichen simplex chronicus
Diabetic dermopathy
mcq.e: **Diabetic dermopathy** ('shin spots') presents as small, atrophic, brown pretibial patches, more common with **long-standing diabetes and microvascular complications** (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy). It reflects microangiopathy and poor healing after unnoticed minor trauma. It is harmless, needs no specific treatment and often fades over **18-24 months**.
w: Wrong - necrobiosis lipoidica forms larger yellow-brown waxy plaques with atrophic centres, mostly in type 1 diabetes.
Wrong - pretibial myxoedema is raised, non-pitting peau d'orange plaques in Graves disease.
Wrong - stasis dermatitis is itchy, eczematous and around the medial ankle with venous signs.
Wrong - lichen simplex chronicus is an itchy, thickened plaque from scratching, not asymptomatic atrophic spots.
Correct - small atrophic brown shin patches in long-standing diabetes with microvascular disease are diabetic dermopathy.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has a 2-year-old, well-demarcated, shiny, yellowish-brown plaque on her left shin with a raised red-brown active edge. The centre is atrophic and waxy with visible telangiectasia. There is no ulceration.
Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
o: Intralesional steroid to the active edge, not the atrophic centre
Potent topical steroid under occlusion applied to the whole plaque
Oral flucloxacillin for two weeks to treat a presumed cellulitis
Surgical excision of the plaque with primary closure in clinic
Ketoconazole 2% cream twice daily to the plaque for four weeks
mcq.e: This is established **necrobiosis lipoidica**. Potent topical steroids help **early** lesions, while **intralesional steroids into the active border** treat established plaques. Steroids must be **avoided on the atrophic centre**, which would thin further and ulcerate. Excision heals poorly on the shin and the lesion often recurs.
w: Correct - intralesional steroid to the active border controls established lesions without worsening the atrophic centre.
Wrong - potent steroid over the atrophic centre worsens atrophy and risks ulceration.
Wrong - this is a chronic granulomatous plaque, not an infection.
Wrong - shin wounds in diabetes heal poorly and the lesion may recur in the scar.
Wrong - antifungals have no role; this is not a fungal infection.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has had an ulcer under his right first metatarsal head for 3 weeks. Today a sterile probe passes down to bone, and the adjacent second toe is red, swollen and sausage-shaped. He is afebrile, and his pedal pulses are palpable.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue dressings and offloading, and review in the foot clinic in 2 weeks
Start oral cloxacillin for 1 week and review the wound afterwards
Apply topical metronidazole gel and continue daily dressings
Refer urgently for specialist care for suspected osteomyelitis
Arrange a routine vascular surgical clinic appointment
mcq.e: A positive **probe-to-bone** test and a red 'sausage' toe point to **osteomyelitis**. The CPG lists **clinical concern of deep-seated tissue or bone infection** as an **urgent referral**, alongside sepsis, critical limb ischaemia and gangrene. The absence of fever does not exclude it: neuropathy and diabetes blunt the systemic response.
w: Wrong - routine review delays treatment of a deep bone infection.
Wrong - a short oral course cannot treat osteomyelitis, which needs imaging, cultures and prolonged therapy.
Wrong - topical antimicrobials do not reach bone infection.
Correct - suspected osteomyelitis is a deep-seated infection requiring urgent specialist referral.
Wrong - pulses are palpable, so ischaemia is not the main problem, and routine referral is too slow.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes cannot feel the 10 g monofilament at several sites on both feet. She usually wears thong slippers (selipar) at home and to the market, and asks what she should wear instead.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Thong slippers are fine if she checks her feet every evening
Snug, tight-fitting shoes to stop her feet sliding and rubbing
Covered, breathable shoes, checked inside before each wearing
Walking barefoot at home to let the skin of her feet breathe
Open sandals with a hard sole, as long as the toes are free
mcq.e: With loss of protective sensation, she will not feel injury. The CPG advises **covered shoes with breathable material**, correctly fitting (not too tight or too loose), and **checking footwear for foreign or penetrating objects** before and after wearing. **Thong slippers** and barefoot walking expose the feet to unnoticed trauma.
w: Wrong - thong slippers are specifically discouraged; daily checks do not prevent the injury.
Wrong - shoes that are too tight cause pressure ulcers on insensate feet.
Correct - covered, breathable, well-fitting shoes checked inside before use protect a neuropathic foot.
Wrong - barefoot walking risks unnoticed cuts and burns.
Wrong - open sandals leave the toes and sides of the foot unprotected.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years attends his annual review at a Klinik Kesihatan. He has no foot symptoms. His skin is intact and his pedal pulses are palpable.
Which test is the most appropriate screen for loss of protective sensation?
o: Nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs
10 g monofilament at standard plantar sites
Pinprick sensation with a hypodermic needle
Ankle-brachial pressure index with Doppler
Plain X-ray of both feet for Charcot changes
mcq.e: The **10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament**, applied until it buckles at standard plantar sites, is the simple, validated bedside screen for **loss of protective sensation**, ideally with a 128 Hz tuning fork. All people with diabetes need at least **annual foot screening**, with risk category deciding review frequency. ABPI assesses circulation, not sensation.
w: Wrong - nerve conduction studies are not used for routine primary-care screening.
Correct - the 10 g monofilament is the standard screen for loss of protective sensation.
Wrong - a hypodermic needle can break the skin; sharp testing uses a disposable neurotip, and it is not the main screen.
Wrong - ABPI assesses peripheral arterial disease, not neuropathy.
Wrong - X-rays are for suspected Charcot foot or osteomyelitis, not sensory screening.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents with firm, non-pitting, raised, yellowish-brown plaques on both shins with prominent hair follicles giving a peau d'orange appearance. They are neither itchy nor painful. She has lost weight, has a fine tremor and her eyes look prominent.
Which test is most likely to identify the underlying cause?
o: Thyroid function and TSH-receptor antibodies
HbA1c and fasting lipid profile
Doppler ultrasound of the leg veins
Serum albumin and urine protein-creatinine ratio
Skin scraping for KOH microscopy
mcq.e: Non-pitting peau d'orange shin plaques with weight loss, tremor and proptosis are **pretibial myxoedema** of **Graves disease** (triad: dermopathy, ophthalmopathy, thyroid acropachy). **TSH-receptor antibodies** activate fibroblasts to deposit glycosaminoglycans in the dermis. Despite its name, it is not a feature of hypothyroid 'myxoedema'.
w: Correct - thyroid function and TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves disease, the cause of pretibial myxoedema.
Wrong - HbA1c targets necrobiosis lipoidica, which is waxy and atrophic, not peau d'orange with thyrotoxic features.
Wrong - venous disease causes pitting oedema and stasis eczema, not non-pitting plaques.
Wrong - nephrotic oedema is soft and pitting.
Wrong - these plaques are not fungal.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man has a 2 cm smooth, round, firm-to-fluctuant swelling on his upper back that has grown slowly over 2 years. It is attached to the overlying skin, which shows a small dark central pore, and it moves with the skin over the deeper tissues. Squeezing it once released foul-smelling, cheesy material.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subcutaneous lipoma
Dermatofibroma
Keratoacanthoma
Epidermoid cyst
Furuncle (boil)
mcq.e: An **epidermoid (so-called sebaceous) cyst** is **fixed to the skin**, has a **central punctum** and contains **keratin** (cheesy, smelly material). A **lipoma** is soft, lobulated, lies beneath the skin, which moves freely over it, and has no punctum. Cysts are excised with their whole wall to prevent recurrence.
w: Wrong - a lipoma is soft and lobulated with the skin moving freely over it and no punctum.
Wrong - a dermatofibroma is a small, firm dermal nodule that dimples on pinching, with no punctum or contents.
Wrong - a keratoacanthoma grows rapidly over weeks with a central keratin crater, not slowly over years.
Correct - a skin-fixed lump with a central punctum and keratin contents is an epidermoid cyst.
Wrong - a furuncle is acute, hot and tender, not a slow 2-year swelling.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has a 7 mm firm, brownish, button-like nodule on her lower leg that appeared some months after an insect bite. It is mildly itchy and has not changed for a year. When the skin on either side is squeezed together, the lesion dimples inwards.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Nodular melanoma
Seborrhoeic keratosis
Epidermoid cyst
Keloid scar
Dermatofibroma
mcq.e: A **dermatofibroma** is a common benign fibrous nodule (about 7-10 mm), usually on the **limbs**, often after minor trauma such as a bite. The **dimple sign** on lateral pinching is characteristic. Management is **reassurance**, with simple excision only if the patient wishes. Change in size, colour or bleeding would prompt referral to exclude melanoma.
w: Wrong - nodular melanoma grows, may bleed and does not show the dimple sign.
Wrong - seborrhoeic keratoses are stuck-on, warty, pitted surface lesions, not firm dermal nodules.
Wrong - an epidermoid cyst has a punctum and cystic contents and bulges rather than dimples.
Wrong - a keloid is a scar extending beyond the original wound and does not dimple.
Correct - a firm limb nodule with a positive dimple sign is a dermatofibroma.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man who works outdoors has a 1.5 cm dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater on his forearm. It appeared and grew rapidly over 5 weeks. There is no regional lymphadenopathy.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and review in 3 months, since most will involute by then
Excise with histology, as it can mimic squamous cell carcinoma
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen without taking a biopsy
Topical 5-fluorouracil cream for 4 weeks, then review
Oral cloxacillin for a presumed deep follicular infection
mcq.e: A rapidly growing crateriform nodule on sun-damaged skin is a **keratoacanthoma**, but it **cannot be reliably distinguished from well-differentiated SCC** clinically. The lesion should be **excised with histology**; curettage is acceptable only if the diagnosis is certain, and lesions on the lip or ear are treated as SCC.
w: Wrong - although some regress, waiting risks missing a squamous cell carcinoma.
Correct - excision with histology both treats it and excludes squamous cell carcinoma.
Wrong - destroying the lesion without tissue loses the chance to exclude SCC.
Wrong - topical 5-FU treats actinic keratoses, not an undiagnosed rapidly growing nodule.
Wrong - this is a keratinising tumour, not an infection.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old man with dark skin has a firm, shiny, raised, itchy scar on his earlobe that developed 4 months after ear piercing. It has spread well beyond the original puncture site and is still enlarging.
What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Simple surgical excision alone, with no adjuvant therapy
Reassure; it will flatten and fade fully within 1 year
Intralesional corticosteroid injections into the scar
Oral antibiotics for a presumed infected granuloma
Cryotherapy then re-piercing through the same site
mcq.e: A scar that **extends beyond the original wound margin** is a **keloid** (a hypertrophic scar stays within it). Keloids are commoner in dark skin and rarely regress. First-line options are **intralesional corticosteroid injections** and **compression or silicone dressings**. Excision alone has a high recurrence rate, so surgery is combined with adjuvant steroid or pressure.
w: Wrong - excision alone often produces a larger recurrent keloid.
Wrong - keloids rarely regress; spontaneous flattening is more typical of hypertrophic scars.
Correct - intralesional steroid injection is a first-line treatment for an active keloid.
Wrong - there is no infection; antibiotics do not treat excess collagen.
Wrong - re-traumatising the same site provokes further keloid formation.
